The plan for the whole isle war was called Operation Forager. Source lists and a note on the set close the book.

Landings in the north and on the south shores start the fight. Chonito Cliff, Fonte Ridge, and Orote fall one by one. War dogs, a famed side arm, and medal men fill side tales. The push north ends the foe's hold on the isle. War past fans get a tight, clear tale.
49384-selling-home-furnishings-a-trainin:
Selling Home Furnishings is a training program for furniture salesmen, issued in 1941 as a bulletin of the United States Office of Education. It was prepared by Roscoe Rau of the National Retail Furniture Association and Walter Shaw, a regional agent of the business education service. The government printing office sold it for seventy five cents.

Unit one presents the salesman as a business builder: specialized selling as a career, increasing sales and earnings, and a daily check up. Unit two teaches technique: sale objectives, starting the simple sale, the all important interview, and closing. Unit three applies salesmanship: how to demonstrate values, the contrast in buying methods of women and men, and enriching your vocabulary. Vocational bulletins like this one trained the retail army of wartime America.
50169-hermia-suydam:
Hermia Suydam, a novel by Gertrude Franklin Atherton, was copyrighted in 1889 and issued at New York. Atherton had written What Dreams May Come before this book. The tale opens in a Second Avenue household in the city. John Suydam gives his blessing in the second chapter.

Brooklyn and Babylon stand as a chapter head, for the two worlds of the tale. The green room of literature gives Hermia a stage of another kind. Later heads name the sweets of solitude and a legacy left by Suydam. Hermia discovers herself as the story grows, by the eighth chapter. A tailor made fate and a club of free souls mark the later turns. The novel studies a young woman of means who seeks a life of her own.
51053-judas-ram:
Sam Merwin wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in December 1950. Drawings by James Vincent ran with the story. Its odd house, furnished with all luxuries, stands at the center of the tale.

Roger Tennant crosses the lawn and studies the house's three wings. They spread spoke-like from a seven-sided center, each in a different style. One wing mimics the old Deep South, one is a slick modern sun house, and one rises spired and gabled like old Cracow. Dana waits for him under a tree. Readers get a strange tale of wealth and hidden purpose from a slick magazine hand.
51842-beyond-bedlam:
Wyman Guin imagines a turned world in Beyond Bedlam, from Galaxy Science Fiction in August 1951, with pictures by David Stone. A prefatory note warns that the society so elaborately described has its seeds in ours, and bids the reader check the data. The tale opens in an ego-shifting class.

Mary Walden watches Carl Blair caught passing a limerick about a hyper who keeps a third head for a thrill. Called on herself, Mary recites her pharmacy history lesson. Schizophrenia, she explains, is where two or more personalities live in one brain. The ancients of the twentieth century, she says, shamefully locked such people up as crazy.
53236-a-thanksgiving-dream:
Effa Preston wrote A Thanksgiving Dream, a one-act play for children. The Paine company at Dayton, Ohio, sold it for twenty-five cents. It is marked as a play for primary children on its title. Song specialties for entertainments are advertised at the front. Welcome songs and closing songs fill those lists with titles.

Jack, a small boy, heads the cast of characters. Five pilgrim maids stand in the cast beside him. Jack sings of the grandest dinner in the play's verse. Pudding and cake and pie, turkey and mashed potato, he lists. Ice cream makes him sigh to think of the feast, he says. Teachers are discovering that songs hold an audience, the ads urge. The words must be clever and the music catchy, they add. Preston gives a schoolroom Thanksgiving piece with songs.
53317-the-novel-on-the-tram:
The Novel on the Tram, by Galdos, is a Spanish story in a translation by Michael Wooff. Wooff granted his English version to the public domain for all readers. The tram left the end of the Salamanca district to cross Madrid, it begins. Its route runs through the whole city in the direction of Pozas.

The narrator grabs the handrail to sit down before others with the same intention. At the same time he collides with another passenger on the other side. He looks and knows his friend Don Dionisio Cascajares at once in that crash. A warm and enthusiastic handshake follows the fateful meeting on the platform. A tale spun inside a tram ride shows Galdos art in miniature here.
5335-raspberry-jam:
Carolyn Wells's Raspberry Jam is a detective novel featuring Fleming Stone, opening with a dispute over telepathy and mind reading. Aunt Abby insists there is something in mind reading, while Eunice warns that if she keeps on, she may say what she thinks. The argument sets the tone for a mystery of séances and mediums.

Chapters follow the great Hanlon, a trip to Newark, a stunt, the Emburys, a slammed door, a vision. Marigny the medium appears, as Stone sorts truth from trickery. Readers get a lively period mystery, with Wells's usual mix of humour, suspects. The detective trusts evidence over the supernatural.
54453-beyond-the-hills-of-dream:
Beyond the Hills of Dream is a book of poems by Wilfred Campbell, published at Boston in 1899. Campbell dedicates the volume to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, prime minister of Canada. The title poem opens the book. It calls the beloved over the mountains of sleep and dream. Beyond the walls of care and fate lies a world of fancy. There hearts forget to weep and meet the long lost dead.

Morning pieces and shore pieces fill the early pages. Out of Pompeii and Bereavement of the Fields show his range. A September poem is set in the Laurentian Hills of Canada. Lazarus, The Mother, and The Last Prayer bring in sacred themes. Poems on England, Victoria, and Sebastian Cabot turn to empire and history. To the Ottawa closes the Canadian strain of the book.
54930-little-snap-the-postboy-or-working:
Little Snap, the Postboy, or Working for Uncle Sam, is a boys' adventure novel by Victor St Clair, printed in 1903. St Clair also wrote Cast Away in the Jungle and For Home and Honor. The hero is a young postboy who rides the mail in the Kanawha country. The chapter list promises missing mail, a terrific trap, and a curious court.

The story follows Little Snap through arrests, lonely night rides, and perilous undertakings. Chapters tell of registered letters, a bushbinder's plans, and an underground race. The dark bay horse he rides is praised as a fine specimen from the Blue Grass regions. The horse knows the road so well that it halts where its rider will be challenged. The book is a dime-novel style tale of pluck and duty on the mail routes, written to thrill boy readers of its day.
55868-lady-william:
Mrs. Oliphant wrote this tale, first put out in three books in January 1894. A cheap shape in one book came out that May. The tale opens in the town of Watcham. It is not a town in the plain sense of the word, the first page says, yet it is a sweet place. Folk who come on its small pier by the stream, or drive through its old green, call it a sweet town at sight.

Some of its homes look as if they had stepped out of the age two past, and some as if from the books of cuts for the young. It is a town of fine small homes. In them live a great count of folk who have claims to rank but are poor. Some have no such claims and are poor all the same.
57208-the-jew-the-gypsy-and-el-islam:
Sir Richard F Burton, explorer and translator of the Arabian Nights, left these studies, edited after his death by W H Wilkins and published at London in 1898. A portrait by Lord Leighton fronts the book. Burton died before the work could be finished.

The first study weighs the Jew: opinion of him in general and in England, the Jew of the Holy Land, and the Talmud. The second takes up the Gypsy, his Indian affinities, and modern studies, then maps the Gypsies of Europe, Asia, and Africa. El Islam forms the third part. The book is Burton at his most learned and most combative, on peoples he had lived among.
57253-peeps-at-many-lands-siam:
Peeps at Many Lands: Siam is one small volume of a children's travel series published at London by Adam and Charles Black. Each volume holds twelve full page illustrations in color and sells for a shilling and sixpence. The series list runs from Burma and Canada to Japan, Morocco, and the South Seas, with a fat volume on the whole world.

The Siam volume shows young readers the kingdom now called Thailand: its rivers, temples, elephants, and kings. Such series taught geography by story and picture before film and radio. A child of 1910 could peep at Siam from a nursery chair. The color plates did much of the teaching. The book is a neat sample of how empire age Britain pictured the wider world for its young.
57265-the-ra-ma-yana-volume-1-ba-laka-nd:
The Ramayana of Valmiki was Englished in prose from the Sanskrit and printed at Calcutta in 1891, edited and published by Manmatha Nath Dutt of Keshub Academy. Volume one holds the Balakandam and the Ayodhyakandam, the books of the hero's youth and of Ayodhya. The full set cost sixteen rupees in India and two pounds in Europe, postage paid, the front pages say.

The immortal epic of Valmiki is one of the gems of literature, the preface cries, the very Kohinur of the literary region. For ages it has shed a matchless light from a dim and far past. Rama's birth, boyhood, marriage, and the throne plot that sends him to the forest fill these two books. Dutt's plain prose made the great Indian epic readable for English readers in India and abroad.
57468-a-group-of-eastern-romances-and-st:
Clouston gathered eastern romances and stories from the Persian, Tamil, and Urdu, privately printed in 1889 in an edition of three hundred copies. Clouston had edited the Book of Sindibad and the Bakhtyar Nama. Who is he, overcome with idleness or worldly cares, that will not be lightened by reading some enticing story, true or feigned, Burton is quoted.

Clouston gives the book to Forster Fitzgerald Arbuthnot of the Royal Asiatic Society. You have always been warmly interested in my works and in Oriental literature generally, he writes. No man is more able to appreciate their value for the comparative study of popular fictions, he says. In the unchanging East, old tales still reflect the habits of races when they were made. Folk tale scholars get rare versions here.
58097-reminiscences-of-tottenham:
Couchman wrote Reminiscences of Tottenham, a short account of a London parish as it was in her childhood. The book was transcribed from an edition of about 1909. She had lived in the parish all her life, and friends kept asking her to set down her early recollections before they were lost.

Her father was born at Palmers Green in 1798 and her mother in Tottenham in 1800, and they married at All Hallows Church in 1825. The Tottenham of her youth was a village of meadows, cornfields, and lanes under stately elms. Every inhabitant was known to every other in that small world. Her plain tale keeps the old village in mind as the city swallowed it.
59979-glen-canyon-dam:
Glen Canyon Dam is a government booklet of facts and figures from the Bureau of Reclamation, issued under Interior Secretary Stewart Udall. It gives the dam in hard numbers first: a concrete arch, seven hundred ten feet from its lowest foundation, with a crest fifteen hundred feet long. The concrete in dam and power house runs past five million cubic yards. Comparisons with Hoover and Grand Coulee dams set the scale.

Behind the dam, Lake Powell, named for the explorer John Wesley Powell, was to hold a vast store of Colorado River water. The figures give its length as one hundred eighty six miles and its power plant at nine hundred thousand kilowatts in eight units. The dam stands in Arizona, thirteen river miles below the Utah line, as the key work of the Upper Colorado storage plan. The booklet is the project in brief.
60064-dorothea-beale-of-cheltenham:
Elizabeth Raikes wrote this life of Dorothea Beale, published by Constable in London in 1908. Beale, born on March 21, 1831, into a Gloucestershire family, became the best known head of the Cheltenham Ladies' College. Raikes tells the story in Beale's own words wherever she can.

Chapters move from childhood through Queen's College and a teaching post at Casterton to the Cheltenham years. They cover the early history of the Ladies' College, a royal commission, the work of organisation, hard years, the Guild, and Hilda's work at Oxford. Letters and a final term close the book. It records how one woman built a great girls' school and shaped the schooling of women in Victorian England.
60188-the-ra-ma-yana-volume-3-yuddhaka-n:
Ramayana, volume three, gives the Yuddha Kandam in English prose. Manmatha Nath Dutt edited and published the translation at Calcutta in 1893. The text renders the Sanskrit epic of Valmiki into plain English prose. Dutt was rector of the Keshub Academy in that city. A transcriber's note explains how macrons mark long vowels in names.

Yuddha means war, and this book covers the great war of the epic. Sections march in order from the first muster to the last fights. Names such as Garuda keep one spelling through the volume for clarity. The Deva Press printed the book at Beadon Street in Calcutta. Readers in English could thus read the climax of Rama's war.
60317-saratoga-national-historical-park-:
Saratoga National Historical Park's Junior Ranger Program is a park activity booklet for young visitors, issued from the park office at 648 Route 32, Stillwater, New York. Opening pages give the ways in. The park stands forty miles north of Albany, off the Northway at exit 12 for the battlefield. Route 29 leads to Schuylerville, for the Schuyler House and Saratoga Monument.

The first activity sends rangers on a scavenger hunt through the park, drawing each find: a cannon, an officer's sword, uniform buttons, a cartridge box, an animal track, a monument. A second activity turns to food and supplies, and how armies of the 1700s took what they needed from civilians. Requisition, payment promised or made in Continental money few would take, is the lesson behind the hunt.
60630-the-log-of-the-ark-by-noah-hierogl:
Two humorists, Gordon and Frueh, dug up The Log of the Ark for Dutton in 1915, crediting Noah as author and Ham as the hand behind its hieroglyphics. A large crowd came down to see us off, says the front picture. The book plays the flood as a modern ocean voyage.

Its Who's Who lists Noah as captain, purser, and veterinarian, with Shem on the wireless and Ham as chief engineer. Wives run the cooking, laundry, and stewardess work. Automatic stokers tend the engines. The joke is steady and gentle: the oldest voyage in scripture, re-run with ship's officers, shore crowds, and a captain's log, in the year when ocean liners filled the papers.
60664-pipe-dream:
Pipe Dream is a science fiction story by Fritz Leiber, first published in Worlds of If in February 1959. Simon Grue is a Greenwich Village artist whose studio skylight overlooks the roof next door. That roof, with its pent shack, water tank and chicken-wire enclosures, has housed bootleggers, Buddhist monks and a fencing salon in its time.

The present tenants are Russians named Stulnikov-Gurevich, four brothers and a sister who never leaves the house. Then Simon finds a two-inch mermaid in his bathtub. It has arms, hips and a finny tail, and a face that reminds him irresistibly of Grushenka, the unseen sister. Only then does he seriously wonder what the Russians are doing on the roof. Leiber mixes Village bohemia, cold war suspicion and a fairy tale in a glass of water.
60685-downstream:
Sigfrid Siwertz wrote this novel, issued in Toronto by the Macmillan Company of Canada in 1923 in the Borzoi-Gyldendal series of Scandinavian books. The series placed it beside works by Knut Hamsun, Sigrid Undset, and Johannes V Jensen. The tale is told in parts, and its chapters bear names such as The Cry, Fear, The Two Fair Heads, and Brundin's Downfall.

A boy named Peter runs through the book, first as watch-dog, then as boss. Laura's marriage, a Spanish saint, and a September spring mark its turns. Siwertz opens with a warning that to tell a child's story as one would a grown man's is a kind of forgery. A dream is hard to report once one is wide awake.
61454-sketches-of-gotham:
Ike Swift wrote Sketches of Gotham, tales of New York low life. Richard K Fox issued the book at New York in 1906. Its tales are told in an unusual way, the title boasts. A photo list of plates fronts the text. Ike Swift's own portrait leads that list. Plate lines tease each tale's spice.

A dance helped one girl meet people, a caption says. Knockout drops turned one life, says another. One girl shipped as a sailor boy on a navy ship. One sat trussed like a chicken for three hours. Hop smoking gets taught for honest dollars in one tale. Atlantic City draws sporty girls in another. Cheap thrills from the sporting press show the city's rough edge as Fox's readers loved it, half shock and half grin.
62026-a-yankee-girl-at-antietam:
Alice Turner Curtis wrote A Yankee Girl at Antietam, published by the Penn Publishing Company in Philadelphia in 1923. Nat Little illustrated it. The book continues Curtis's Yankee Girl series, which had taken its heroines to Fort Sumter, Bull Run, and Shiloh. Here Roxy Delfield stays at her grandmother Miller's farm near the village of Antietam in Maryland, in the September of 1862.

Roxy runs down the path in blue-checked gingham and a broad straw hat. The contents promise paper circuses, signals, and new friends before the war arrives. Then come startling news, Roxy taken prisoner, and her ride to Sharpsburg. The battle of Antietam fills the sixteenth chapter, the bloodiest single day of the Civil War. Curtis wrote history as girls' adventure: the great events seen from a farmhouse by a child who must be brave while armies pass her door.
62033-blood-will-tell-the-strange-story-:
Davenport wrote this novel, subtitled the strange story of a son of Ham. The Caxton Book Company published it at Cleveland in 1902, with illustrations by Donahey. A transcriber's note at the front warns readers that the book carries racial stereotyping unusually unpleasant even by the standards of its time. Its dedication addresses Americans who hold purity of race all-important.

The story opens on a misty November day in Boston, at a house near the wharves where the Dunlap shipping and banking sign has hung since the early republic. The Dunlaps traded with the West Indies, especially Haiti, and ran a line of sailing ships. They christened their sons only with names furnishing the same first letter, so the house name never changed. The frontispiece shows the brutalized features of Walter Burton, and the picture list promises Lucy, her grandfather, and a reckless rush in front of Burton.
62052-bailey-s-dam:
Bailey's Dam is an archaeological study published by the state of Louisiana in 1986. It is Anthropological Study number eight in its series. The Louisiana Archaeological Survey and Antiquities Commission issued it. A cover note explains the printing cost and run of the document. Ninety five hundred copies were printed in this first printing. The Division of Archaeology published it at Baton Rouge. An illustration shows Porter's fleet passing the dam at Alexandria. That picture comes from Harper's Pictorial History of the Civil War.

It is dated May 1864 in that source's pages. Bailey's Dam was a timber crib dam built in the Red River. Union forces built it to free a stranded fleet in 1864. The study treats the site's history and remains archaeologically. State archaeologists directed the survey behind the report.
62767-the-miller-and-his-golden-dream:
The Miller and His Golden Dream is a moral poem for young readers, printed at Wellington in Shropshire in 1822. Its writer had earlier written The Ruby Ring and kindred tales with genii and magic aids. Here she lays those aids aside on purpose, holding that a moral truth needs little show to draw the young.

A verse at the front sets the theme: be content with moderate blessings, for peace and a life well spent are treasures that cannot fade. The poem itself opens on avarice, called the deadliest passion of the breast. It hardens and shrinks the heart, the poet warns, and the miller's golden dream shows what that vice costs.
62989-jimmy-kirkland-of-the-cascade-coll:
Hugh S Fullerton wrote Jimmy Kirkland of the Cascade College Team, published by the John C Winston Company at Philadelphia in 1915. Charles Paxson Gray drew the illustrations. Fullerton inscribed the book to Amos Alonzo Stagg, player, coach, and teacher. Stagg had made honesty in college sport a reality, the dedication says. The first chapter brings the new man to Cascade. The college stands on a plateau in California sunshine.

Larry clashes with the coach and seeks revenge in the early chapters. Krag reads him a lesson, and a friend is found in the foe's camp. A pig in the parlor raises the Peeg excitement midway, and the mystery is cleared. Helen falls into trouble, and a treacherous blow lands. The game with Golden, the captain of Cascade, and temptation follow. The final game closes the tale.
62990-islam:
Annie Small wrote this short study of Islam, published in London in 1905 as the second number in a series called Studies in the Faiths. She had already written on Buddhism and on Hindu themes. A picture of the Pearl Mosque at Agra faces the title page.

The editor's note warns modern readers that parts of the book show the prejudice of Christians of her day toward Islam. That honesty makes the book doubly useful: it tells the faith's story as a fair minded Edwardian could learn it, and it shows the lens she looked through. Small writes for the general reader who wanted the world's faiths in brief, clear accounts. The series gave each faith the same plain treatment.
6363-life-is-a-dream:
Denis Florence Mac-Carthy translates Calderon's dramas fully from Spanish in the metre of the original, in an 1873 London volume from Henry S. King. Two dramas here are Calderon's most celebrated, and the first, La Vida es Sueno, has been played with success on almost every European stage except England's. In Moscow in the winter of 1866 to 1867 it drew crowded houses, and in Stockholm a queen expired in the theatre during its performance.

Mac-Carthy's introduction calls the play much studied in England for literary value and lyrical beauty, even where it was not staged. Clorilene bears a son under prodigies of heaven, and the verse that follows, in Mac-Carthy's metre, tells of fate, knowledge, and a man injured by what he knows. The book gives English readers Calderon as poetry, not only as plot, in a translation that keeps his music.
64056-the-peril-and-the-preservation-of-:
The Peril and the Preservation of the Home is a set of talks by Riis, the famed Dane who fought the slums of New York. They were the years talks of a named fund, in the first years of the last age. He had writ past books on his own make in America and on the war with the slum.

It came out at Philadelphia that same spring. A note at its front tells of a print form on the web with its first pictures. Its case is told in its name. The home is the root of the land, he holds, and the slum flat is its rot: crowd, foul air, and no room for a child to grow straight. Its cure is light, air, law, and the care of the town.
64265-crash-beam:
John Barret wrote "Crash Beam," a science fiction story printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1947. Its blurb hangs on the hero's dread. Dan Kearns, sick and shaking, could already hear them talk. Come in on the Kearns beam, they would say: it is a new way to die.

The crash comes in the first paragraph. One instant the big Earth to Venus rocket freighter was sizzling through the fog to a perfect landing below. Then she dipped, undershot the field, and vanished in a flash and a thundering explosion. In the dreamlike quiet Dan Kearns heard the faint yells of the landing crew. Searchlights cut wide swaths through the boiling fog, and white coated medics ran across the light. Kearns, the beam's own man, sat down feeling sick. The tale turns on blame and the fear of a name becoming a joke told at funerals.
64648-the-green-dream:
The Green Dream is a science fiction story by Bryce Walton, first printed in the magazine Planet Stories in the winter of 1949. Its headnote sets the conflict: Owen Baarslag had brought terror to the swamp people, and Joha, the little Venusian maid, was determined that he should not leave without it.

Joha, who is part Venusian, twines her translucent fingers through the sleeping Earthman's matted hair. Her face is light green, and her red eyes shine with hatred and a malignant purpose, but only while he sleeps. The man lies on a couch of lizard skin softened with feathers from the Kuh-Kuri swampbird, twitching in a growing nightmare. Around them lies the fetid heart of the Venusian swamp, Sector Five, where a serpent hisses in the slime and a great flying creature falls on its prey. Walton builds the tale on her unseen revenge.
64863-lie-on-the-beam:
Lie on the Beam is a science fiction story by John Victor Peterson, from the magazine Comet of March 1941. A transcriber note says the text was produced from that issue of the magazine. No renewal of the publication copyright was found, the note adds for the reader. The tale opens in space, with a black destroyer sweeping from perihelion toward Venus.

Its jets stab mocking fingers at the sun whose gravity the ship has cheated in its flight. Within the shielded control cabin, the commander hard skull face splits into a fleshless smile on the page. From his fanged jaws a single word is spat into the intercom system of the ship. The word, Adrakolarn, had been a weak dream word on dead sea bottoms in the tale past. Peterson story is pulp space opera of the purest kind, all Venus, destroyers, and dying worlds.
65588-the-evacuation-of-england-the-twis:
Gratacap wrote The Evacuation of England, a scientific romance printed in New York in 1908. Its premise is a twist in the Gulf Stream, the great ocean current that keeps Britain mild. Set in 1909 and 1910, the tale imagines the stream failing and the cold falling on England like a sentence.

Chapters open in Washington, move to a lecture and to Gettysburg, then cross to the eviction of Scotland and a London in terror. The evacuation itself closes the tale, as a nation takes ship from its frozen island. Gratacap, a geologist by trade, built his warning on real science of currents and climate. It is an early tale of climate disaster.
66509-myths-and-folk-lore-of-the-timiska:
Speck's Myths and Folk-lore of the Timiskaming Algonquin and Timagami Ojibwa came out at Ottawa in 1915 as Memoir 71 of the Geological Survey of Canada, in its anthropological series. The Government Printing Bureau issued it under the Department of Mines.

Chapter one follows the Wiskedjak cycle: the trickster pursues the Beaver, gets his head fastened in the Bear's skull, invites the Ducks to a dance and disguises himself as a Lynx. The tales are given with Algonquin text and a free translation, then short lore on the Windigo, the Northern Lights, the Milky Way and the bear feast. Chapter two turns to Nenebuc the transformer, whose Giant Lynx brings the World Flood while Muskrat dives for the earth of a new world.
66566-the-history-of-philosophy-in-islam:
The History of Philosophy in Islam, by de Boer of the University of Groningen, reached English readers in Edward Jones's translation. Luzac and Company published it in London in 1903. De Boer notes in his preface that his book is the first attempt since Munk's sketch to present the subject in connected form. He calls it a fresh beginning rather than a finished task, and thanks the scholars whose work on the sources guided him.

The history follows thought in the Islamic world from its Greek inheritances through its great system builders. It treats schools, translations, and the slow shaping of doctrine. A monograph on Ibn Sina appeared while the book was in press. De Boer judged that it extended his survey without changing it. The volume long served students as the standard short road into its field.
67031-a-letter-to-the-parishioners-of-fu:
Baker, vicar of Fulham, wrote this letter to his parishioners on October 29, 1849, after cholera's second visit to the parish; it sold at fourpence. In 1832, he reminds them, only two Fulham deaths were traced to the disease. In the nine weeks ending October 8 of this year there were 127 deaths in all, more than four times the average, and 56 of them were certified as cholera.

Its speed fills his pages: in 35 cases the illness lasted under twenty-four hours, and in 18 under twelve. Fifty-eight of the dead were aged five to fifty-five, the ages least open to death. Nearly all the cholera dead, he notes with three exceptions only, were of the parish's poorest class: labourers, and their wives, widows, and children. The letter is at once a parish report and a pastoral reckoning with a visitation.
67238-still-william:
Richmal Crompton continues the mischief of William Brown in a story book first issued in London in April 1925. Thomas Henry drew the pictures, and the book was reprinted many times within five years. The opening tale turns on a silk handkerchief, huge and bright with green dragons on a red ground.

William leads a gang who call themselves the Outlaws, with Ginger, Henry, and Douglas as his fellows. Chapters show William turning over a new leaf, trying blackmail, making money, match-making, and spoiling a party. Violet Elizabeth, who lisps and insists on joining in, crosses his path more than once. Readers get schoolboy plots, schemes gone wrong, and humor that has kept the William books in print for decades.
67774-anne-feversham:
Anne Feversham is a historical novel by Snaith, published by Appleton and Company in New York and London in 1914. In England it appeared as The Great Age. Its first chapter brings William Shakespeare himself on stage, in the prime of his career.

Shakespeare, a distinguished member of the Lord Chamberlain's company, entered a tailor's shop in Nottingham. He is about thirty five, of middle height, with a compact, vigorous figure. His hair is worn rather long, his beard inclining to red, and his dress is plainer than an actor's should be. Only his vivid pallor and somber, slow-burning eyes betray the player. He compliments Master Tidey on a choice coffin-cloth, then turns to grim news. It seems a pity, he says, for a man to die by the ax in the heat of his youth, though better than the string. A gentleman's death, the Queen is giving him.
68047-off-the-beam:
George O Smith wrote this science fiction story for Astounding Science-Fiction, where it appeared in February 1944. The scene is the Solar Queen, a spaceship thirty hours out from Mars and bound for Earth. Guide beams from a relay station hold the ship on course, but the link works one way only.

Don Channing, the Director of Communications, rides aboard and can hear messages but cannot answer them. As the beams bombard the ship with talk meant for him, he turns over a bold idea: a way to reach the relay station from a ship in flight. The story mixes space travel with the nuts and bolts of radio work.
68211-gold-and-glory-or-wild-ways-of-oth:
Grace Stebbing tells a tale of early American discovery in a pictured book issued at New York. In a wry introduction Stebbing apologizes for all writers of historical tales at once. She pleads that her faults never went so far as bending a single fact or adding false color to the record.

Chapter titles run from conspirators in Aragon to Cortes burning his ships and the road to Mexico. The cacique Hatuey, the massacre at Caonao, a rescued human sacrifice, and a pilot in storms mark the darker turns. Don Alonzo steps forward midway, and Montoro threads through the later chapters. Young readers get the Spanish conquest told as adventure, with its gold and its cruelty both kept in view.
68466-building-a-championship-football-t:
Paul W Bear Bryant wrote on building a championship football team. Prentice-Hall issued the book at Englewood Cliffs, with rights from 1960. Bryant led football at the University of Alabama when he wrote. The hosted form is the eighth printing, from February 1968.

A front sketch calls Bryant a teacher of hard-nosed, all-out football. At Texas A and M his teams won 25, lost 14, and tied 2 in four years. John David Crow, his Heisman back, says Bryant made a man of him. Coaches gain a famed winner's plain talk on men, work, and will.
68587-journal-of-william-h-richardson-a-:
William H Richardson kept a journal as a private soldier in the Mexican campaign. John W Woods printed the second form at Baltimore in 1848. Richardson served under Colonel Doniphan of Missouri in New and Old Mexico. A plate shows the march through a jornada, or waterless stretch.

He left West River, Maryland, in November 1845 on a southern tour, he writes. A flag gift and speeches on July 4 fired him to join mounted volunteers. Daily notes track marches, lost trails, and kind hosts from the first days. Readers gain a foot soldier's own fresh record of a famed hard march.
68730-exploration-team:
Exploration Team is a science fiction story by Murray Leinster, from Astounding of March 1956. Emsh illustrated this tale of a felon filed deep in paper work on Loren Two. A jagged nearer moon, probably a captured asteroid, hurtles over the colony world. Huyghens has seen it too often to go out and watch it cross.

Instead he sweats over paper work, though technically a felon for all his labours. A huge bald eagle dozes untethered on a three inch perch in his room. His only assistant has tangled with a night creature as the tale opens. Leinster pairs desk comedy with real danger in this colony story.
68907-the-true-prophecies-or-prognostica:
The True Prophecies of Michael Nostradamus appears here in the old English translation of Theophilus de Garencieres. Ratcliffe and Thompson printed it at London in the sixteen seventies. The title page styles Nostradamus physician to three kings of France. It calls him one of the best astronomers that ever were, and the work full of curiosity and learning.

Garencieres, a French doctor settled in London, translated the quatrains and commented on them. Nostradamus had published his verses of prophecy in the previous century, in a dark Provençal French that invited decoding. Kings, wars, plagues, and the fate of France fill the centuries of verses. Each generation since has found its own face in them. This edition, with its long title page listing a dozen booksellers, shows the prophet already a trade: curiosity for the buyer, learning for the annotator, and riddles for everyone.
69079-memorials-of-old-durham:
Henry R Leighton edited Memorials of Old Durham, published in London in 1910 in a series on the memorials of the counties of England. The volume is dedicated, by his leave, to the Earl of Durham. A frontispiece shows Durham Cathedral from a picture by Turner.

Many hands wrote the chapters. Henry Gee gives a historical introduction, and M Hope Dodds the topography. Other chapters treat the folklore and legends of the county, and the place names of the Durham dales. William Greenwell writes on the cathedral, and others on Finchale Priory, on Monkwearmouth and Jarrow, and on the parish churches. Castles and halls, monumental inscriptions, and the old families of Durham follow. A chapter even traces John Wesley's links with the county. Such county memorials were made to stir local pride and to save fading lore.
69276-the-story-of-islam:
Story of Islam is a survey by Theodore R W Lunt, a missionary education officer. The hosted copy is the third edition, revised, dated nineteen sixteen. Lunt had served the Church Missionary Society in education work. A photo of evening prayer serves as frontispiece, with the line that Islam was born in the desert. The book is dedicated to the public schoolboys of Great Britain.

In his preface to this edition Lunt says it felt strange to revise the book in barracks. He was learning to fire big guns there, possibly against the Turks. That need only underlines the duty to understand the real problem of Islam, he argues. When the war is over, Islam will remain, he writes. Those now at school will have the greater task after, he tells his readers.
69994-the-triumphs-of-perseverance-and-e:
Examples for the young fill this book of lives, published by Darton in London. Portraits of Salvator Rosa and Michael Angelo stand at the front of the volume. Lines from Longfellow promise that lives of great men remind us we may make our own lives sublime.

The preface says the records aim to fire young readers with emulation for good work. Toil in the peaceful fields of science and benevolence is the path held up there. Whatever man has done, man may do, runs the adage quoted. Linguists open the contents, with Sir William Jones among the first triumphs of perseverance.
70429-the-radio-girls-on-the-program:
Margaret Penrose wrote The Radio Girls on the Program, or Singing and Reciting at the Sending Station, published at New York by Cupples and Leon. The catalog title is the book's subtitle, and it dates the volume to 1922. Penrose also wrote the Dorothy Dale and Motor Girls series.

The three Roselawn girls sing their trio in the frontispiece, at the sending station itself. Radio was brand new when the book appeared, and a program at a station was a thrill in itself. The Radio Girls books put modern girls inside the newest technology of their day. Earlier volumes set them at Roselawn and on Station Island. This one puts them on the air, voices out over the ether to unseen listeners.
70829-for-the-good-of-the-team:
For the Good of the Team is a school sports novel by Ralph Henry Barbour, in the Yardley Hall series. The title page places the tale among Barbour school stories at Yardley Hall. Sister books in that series shown at the front are Fourth Down, Forward Pass, and Double Play. Winning His Y, Guarding the Goal, and For Yardley stand with them in the list.

Barbour other series fill the page beside it: the Purple Pennant, Hilton, Erskine, Big Four, Grafton, and North Bank books. The title of this tale states its moral in the open for its readers. The good of the team comes before the glory of the single player in the Yardley code. Barbour heroes learn that lesson on the field each season, in games where the score matters less than the spirit in which the school plays it together.
70950-in-memoriam: The volume titled In Memoriam opens, in this copy, with a publisher's list dated February 1850: the books of Edward Moxon of Dover Street. Haydn's Dictionary of Dates heads it, then histories of Egypt and Florence, the works of Walter Savage Landor, and Dana's Seaman's Manual. The list is the trade wrapper of the edition, the advertising matter bound into the book's first issue.
70970-tragedy-in-dedham:
Tragedy in Dedham, by Francis Russell and published in 1962, tells the story of the Sacco-Vanzetti case. The book opens with a remark by Ferris Greenslet, who wished for a long life if only to learn the truth of the case.

A detailed time line runs from the bombings and Red raids of 1919 through the arrest of the two Italian anarchists. Chapters cover the South Braintree holdup and murders, the night of May 5, and the trial at Plymouth. Middle chapters follow the main trial in three parts and the years of appeals that followed. The book ends with the confessions, the Lowell Committee, the executions of August 1927, and the aftermath. Maps, a list of sources, and an index close the volume.
71717-journal-of-a-cruise-of-the-united-:
Hiram Paulding, a lieutenant in the United States Navy, kept a journal of a cruise of the schooner Dolphin among the islands of the Pacific, issued in New York in 1831. A map of the Mulgrave Islands goes with the text. The ship's task was to hunt the mutineers of the whale ship Globe, who had fled to those far isles.

Paulding says the folk of the Mulgraves lived nearer to a state of nature than any people then known. His plain tale gives a close look at their habits, views, and daily ways, from a search that forced a full survey. He claims no art for the book, just a true record of what he saw on a route few ships took.
72120-mr-replogle-s-dream:
Replogle's Dream is a short tale of the days to come by Evelyn Smith. It was first put out in a sheet of such tales in the last month of nineteen fifty six. A note at its head sets its theme in a line. This was a proud day in the life of the new art, that note says. The show would prove that the craft of gears could not beat man.

The tale is set in a hall of art, the last strong fort of the old long ing. That hall was dear in its love of the past. Past the gear made hands who kept it, there was near naught gear made in the place. It was sworn to be more than a mere shop of trade.
72200-little-sunbeam:
Little Sunbeam is a tale for children by Eleanora Stooke, author of Granfer, printed at London and New York. The front picture shows a Cornish flower farm, and Myra Hughes drew it. Fourteen chapters carry the tale from a street mishap through visits in the country to a Christmas close.

The story opens with Peggy, a girl of nine in a shabby blue coat, and her brother Billy at a toy shop window. Peggy is blind, and Billy tells her what he sees, though she longs to see for herself. A knock down in the street starts the chain of events that gives Peggy her name and her place in kind hearts.
73721-sketches-of-the-christian-life-and:
Sketches of the Christian Life and Public Labors of William Miller gives the life of the Advent preacher. James White gathered the material. He drew on the memoir by Sylvester Bliss and on other sources. The Adventist press at Battle Creek printed it in 1875.

Miller taught the second coming of Christ from prophecy. An introduction quotes his publisher's defence of him. The world linked his name with fanaticism, it says. Those who knew him esteemed his mind and honesty. Revivals attended his lectures across the country. Hundreds dated their conversion to his preaching. White holds that the movement fulfilled prophecy. God raised Miller up for a specific work, he argues.
74019-honeymoon-in-bedlam:
Nelson Bond wrote Honeymoon in Bedlam, a tale in a weird magazine of January 1941. Gigantic webs of doom head the story as its teaser line. Those webs run miles in extent and hundreds of feet deep, it says. The tale opens at a wedding the narrator half remembers. A preacher pronounced the pair man and wife in his hearing.

The bride Lorraine smiled sweetly, and Johnny Larkin smirked, dazed. Sabers clanked as the couple walked under an arch of steel. Then came a banquet, drinks, and demands to kiss the bride again. The narrator woke next morning with a mouth like a birdcage's inside. Sam Evans, second mate of the Pegasus, stood grinning at his bedside. You picked the captain up piggy-back, a voice chortles in his memory. Bond gives a space wedding in comic delirium.
7491-de-amicitia-scipio-s-dream:
Cicero's De Amicitia, On Friendship, is one of the great short works of Roman philosophy, and this volume pairs it with Scipio's Dream. Laelius, famed for wisdom, speaks after the death of his friend Scipio, consoling himself with faith in immortality and with the wish that their friendship be remembered forever. True friendship, he argues, can exist only among good men, and it is founded not on need but on nature.

The synopsis lists the essay's themes: truth-telling even when it offends, the arts of flattery, and virtue as the soul of friendship. Scipio's Dream adds a cosmic vision, in which Scipio visits his ancestor and sees the earth from above. Andrew P. Peabody's translation, with introduction and notes, makes both works open to modern readers.
76128-anton-s-last-dream:
Anton Last Dream is a short tale by Edwin Baird, drawn from Weird Tales of May 1937. Its own headnote calls it a brief tale of the dismal success of a scientist experiment. Anton Slezak, a chemist, holds that what man can dream, man can do. He points to flight, to voices sent round the world, and to sight across space.

Each past dream, he argues, has come true in the hands of men of science. Some of his own dreams faded, and some took real form in his laboratory. None was too fantastic for him to put to a bench test there. On the chemist, he liked to say, rests the future growth of mankind.
77088-paul-harley-s-dream:
The writer known as A L O E wrote these two tales for the young, Paul Harley's Dream and Joe's Letter, a New Year's story published at London and Edinburgh. Paul Harley cries that of all days in the week, a Sunday is the worst for New Year's Eve. It stops all fun, all larking, all hope of adventure. The New Year steals in like a thief while one sleeps, unless one goes to a midnight service like that stupid fellow James Barton.

His grandfather Silas, an aged man with his Bible before him, begins a gentle answer, but the boy cuts him short. Paul has been to school and is vain of his learning. One thing he has not learned: to honour his father and mother, grandparents included. The dream of the title does the teaching. It is Sunday school fiction at full strength.
77191-the-movie-boys-under-uncle-sam:
Victor Appleton wrote The Movie Boys Under Uncle Sam, a tale for boys put out at Garden City in 1926. Its short title tells of film work done for the army in war. Appleton had told past tales of the boys in the wilds, under fire, and in a flood. Rights run from 1919 and from 1926.

Blake Stewart and Joe Duncan, friends and mates in film work, open the tale at the front. Shells drop round them as they shoot scenes of the fight. Joe urges a shift to a shell hole at the left for a safe spot. Parts turn on tricks of the lens, death from the sky, and a charge with the tanks. Lost films, a night of fun, and a spell as held men raise the stakes. The close finds the lost films and ends the hunt.
77370-hold-em-wyndham:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote this schoolboy sports novel, published by D. Appleton and Company in 1925. It belongs to his Wyndham series, which also includes The Fighting Scrub and Bases Full. Barbour was one of the most popular writers of school stories in his time, and this volume follows boys at a boarding school where games matter a great deal.

The title is a coach's cry to hold the line, and the story turns on school honor and hard play. A front picture shows a boy named Tom running the race of his life. Readers get football field tension, locker room loyalty, and the small wars of school life. It is a clean, brisk example of the boys' sports fiction of the 1920s.
77718-final-exam:
Final Exam is a science fiction short story by Sam Merwin, printed in the magazine Fantastic Universe with an editor's note praising his warmly human tales of spacemen and their foibles.

Its teaser states the situation plainly: a sturdy bomb shelter was prepared to protect the Great Man from the flying saucers, but he had to see them with his own eyes. Aides, secretary, and bodyguards press him toward the lead-and-graphite shelter beneath his modest Midwestern summer residence. Curiosity, the trait that helped him to the top, wins instead. He questions his Air Force aide while Denver reports half a dozen of the visitors headed directly toward the house at two thousand miles an hour.
77728-the-book-of-ice-cream:
Fisk wrote The Book of Ice-Cream for the Rural Text-Book Series, edited by Bailey and printed for students of farming and dairy work. The series list at the front shows its company, with books on the small grains, plant production, and southern field crops. Ice cream in that set is no joke, since it was a growing farm industry.

Fisk treats milk, cream, freezing, flavor, and the business of making ice cream sound and clean. Farm families and small plants used such books to turn surplus cream into profit. The science is plain and the directions are full. Readers get a window on the dawn of the ice cream trade, when a treat became an industry.
78626-east-of-siam:
Harry Franck, the vagabond traveler, rambled through the five divisions of French Indo-China and wrote this account, published in 1926. He had noticed the little Annamite soldiers in French uniform during the World War, with their brass-topped mushroom hats and black teeth, and curiosity drew him to their home. He sailed to Saigon, saw the ruins of Angkor in Cambodia, and returned overland to Canton.

Later he brought his family to Hanoi and traveled through Laos, the largest and least known of the five divisions. Photographs by Franck fill the book. He writes as a cheerful tramp among French colonials, to whom the book is dedicated. He finds the colony east of Siam a sample of what China might become under foreign rule, and a fine field for a wanderer.
79054-oldham:
Oldham, or Beside All Waters, by Lucy Ellen Guernsey, was published in New York in 1886, from an 1885 copyright. Guernsey wrote Loveday's History and Irish Amy. Her preface calls the book a tale of quiet country life in a New England parish, with its oddities and gains and a little of the tragedy found everywhere. It is meant, she says, for old and young alike.

Guernsey urges neighborhood Bible-class services, held in a home of an evening, as a way to draw back women kept from church by young children and then by habit. Chapters open at a red schoolhouse, with neighborhood news, Kit at home, strangers, and a meeting. Faith, gossip, and parish work shape the gentle tale.
79350-sketches-in-bedlam:
Sketches in Bedlam, printed in London in 1823 by Sherwood, Jones and Company, shows the traits of insanity in one hundred and forty patients of New Bethlem. Its author hides behind the name A Constant Observer. A history of the hospital, its rules, and its forms of admission go with the sketches.

Named cases include Margaret Nicholson, James Hatfield, Patrick Walsh, and Bannister Truelock, with many other striking maniacs moved from Old Bethlem. The preface praises Bethlem as a model for all Europe in regularity, cleanliness, humanity, and skill. It credits a long parliamentary inquiry for sweeping out old errors and cruelties. Force and terror, the editor argues, only deepen the horrors of madness. Mildness, forbearance, and indulgence have taken their place, and the book itself is offered as a novelty to the public.
79717-master-in-sail-steam:
Charles S Morgan told the life of Maine shipmaster Frank Hewitt Peterson for a 1981 meeting. The talk was made for the Maine Maritime Museum at Bath, Maine. Peterson lived from 1876 to 1958 and sailed for near fifty years. Morgan drew on his own notes plus the captain's journals and scrapbook.

Peterson rose from a small coaster to command of great multi-masted schooners. He then moved to steam and at last led the oldest marine society in America. Wreck, fire, storm, war, and hard labor all marked his years at sea. Sea fans gain a full life that spans the age of sail and steam.
869-the-soul-of-nicholas-snyders-or-the-:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this tale of Nicholas Snyders, the miser of Zaandam, and the fate of his soul. Snyders hoards his gold in a Dutch town, counting each coin while life passes him by, until a reckoning comes that money cannot buy off. The story, published in 1908, wears its moral lightly.

Jerome blends folk-tale dread with his usual humour, letting the miser's greed speak for itself. The tale asks what a life spent gathering is worth when the gathering ends. It stands as a neat, dark fable among Jerome's lighter pieces, and a warning against letting wealth harden the heart.
8734-east-of-paris-sketches-in-the-ga-ti:
Miss Betham-Edwards sketches the country east of Paris, through the Gatinais, Bourbonnais, and Champagne, town by town. Melun, Moret-sur-Loing, Bourron, Larchant, Recloses, and Nemours open the route, followed by La Charite-sur-Loire, Pougues, Nevers, Moulins, Souvigny, and Sens. Later chapters reach Arcis-sur-Aube, Rheims, Soulaines, Bar-sur-Aube, St Jean de Losne, and Nancy, before crossing into Germanised Lorraine and Alsace.

Betham-Edwards, a seasoned English traveller in France, writes with a novelist's eye for streets, inns, churches, and local character. Her sketches blend history, anecdote, and personal encounter, at a time when Alsace-Lorraine's fate was fresh news. Readers planning a French journey, or simply armchair travelling, get a leisurely, well-informed companion to a region less visited than Paris or Provence.
954-tom-swift-and-his-war-tank-or-doing-:
Tom Swift does his bit for Uncle Sam in this wartime tale by Victor Appleton, building a war tank for the army. Past memories, Tom's indifference, and Ned's worry open the story, while queer doings and the taunt of slacker spur Tom to work. Detective Rad and a night test put the tank through its paces.

The tank, a runaway giant that bridges gaps and crushes wire, proves its worth in trials that mimic battle. Appleton writes with patriotic energy, praising invention in service of country. The book is a lively Tom Swift war story, from the years when tanks were new and boys followed the war in the papers.
962-the-poems-of-henry-kendall-with-biog:
Henry Kendall wrote these poems of Australia, gathered here with a biographical note by Bertram Stevens. Kendall, a native-born Australian poet who lived from 1841 to 1882, sang of bush, sea, and mountain, and of the sorrows and hopes of colonial life. The edition breaks long lines by metre, as the note explains.

Kendall's verse is musical and melancholy, rooted in the Australian landscape he loved. His best poems, on rivers, forests, and lost friends, made him his country's first notable poet. The volume preserves his work for readers who want the voice of early Australia, tender, lyrical, and haunted by distance.
a-midsummer-night-s-dream:
William Shakespeare's comedy moves between the court of Athens and a wood where fairies rule the night. This text keeps the old spelling of the early printed editions, as the editor's notes explain. Duke Theseus prepares to marry Hippolyta while young lovers Hermia, Lysander, Helena, and Demetrius quarrel over who must wed whom.

In the wood, Oberon and Titania fight over a changeling boy, and Puck's love juice sends every heart after the wrong person. A group of workmen rehearse a sad play about Pyramus and Thisbe and perform it badly and sweetly at the wedding. Dawn sorts the lovers into pairs, and Puck asks the audience's pardon.
anglo-saxon-chronicle-giles-ingram:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is a set of annals kept in Old English at monasteries across England, here in J. A. Giles's translation as revised by James Ingram. The entries run from the Roman invasion to the Norman Conquest and beyond. Monks added year by year, sometimes in a line, sometimes in a small epic.

Battles, kings, comets, famines, and Viking fleets pass in terse sequence. The annal for Cynewulf and Cyneheard breaks into a full tale of loyalty and revenge. Alfred's wars, the martyrdom of archbishops, and the coming of William the Conqueror all stand in their keepers' own words. The Chronicle is England's diary of itself for six hundred years.
before-adam:
Jack London wrote Before Adam, published in book form in 1907 after running as a serial. Its narrator is a modern man troubled since childhood by dreams so real they feel like memories: memories of a life lived before Adam, in a cave-dwelling folk of the Middle Pleistocene. In dreams he is Big-Tooth, a young male of the Folk, growing up among tree nests, water holes, and constant fear.

Big-Tooth's world holds the gentle Folk, the more advanced Fire People with their bows, and the brute Red-Eye, whose killings haunt the tale. London builds the story on the idea that racial memory can pass down the ages. The result is part adventure, part meditation on how far humankind has, and has not, come.
boy-scouts-in-mexico-or-on-guard-with-un:
G. Harvey Ralphson, writing as a scout master, sent his boy patrols to the Mexican border in Boy Scouts in Mexico. The young scouts go by patrol names, Wolf, Black Bear, and Panther, and their vacation turns into border duty with Uncle Sam. Chapters promise signals on the mountain, a strange disappearance, captures, mistaken arrests, and a crime whose story comes out near the end.

Ralphson packs in woodcraft, codes, and patriotic instruction, dedicating the book to American boys and girls in hopes of usefulness and self-reliance. The plot runs through renegades and underground finds toward the Canal Zone. It is early scout fiction at full gallop: earnest, breathless, and sure that a trained boy is a match for any smuggler.
britannica-1911-abbot-william:
William Abbot receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbot, an English actor born in Chelsea in 1798, debuted at Bath in 1806 and in London in 1808. Covent Garden gave him his first firm success in 1813, in light comedy and melodrama.

Pylades to Macready's Orestes marked 1816, when Macready first played that house. Abbot created Appius Claudius in Virginius and Modus in The Hunchback for Sheridan Knowles. In 1827 he took a company with Macready and Miss Smithson to play Shakespeare in Paris. Romeo to Fanny Kemble's Juliet followed in 1830. Two of his own melodramas played Covent Garden. He died in poverty at Baltimore, the entry closes, in 1843.
britannica-1911-abildgaard-nikolaj-abrah: Nikolaj Abraham Abildgaard is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry calls him the Father of Danish Painting. Born at Copenhagen in 1744, son of antiquarian draughtsman Sören Abildgaard, he formed his style on Claude and Poussin. Art, not nature, fed his cold theory, the entry judges. Fine craft and even tone mark his painting, though foreign eyes find it seldom gripping. He founded the Danish school and taught Thorwaldsen and Eckersberg.
britannica-1911-abu-tammam:
Abu Tammam (807-846) was an Arabian poet of the tribe of Tai, born at Jasim, north-east of the Sea of Tiberias. Stories place him selling water in a Cairo mosque as a boy, then trying poetry in Egypt without earning a living. Damascus and Mosul followed, then reward from the governor of Armenia, and after 833 a place at the caliph's court in Baghdad.

Compiling made his lasting name. Abu Tammam gathered early poems into the celebrated collection known as the Hamasa, and two similar collections are also ascribed to him. His own poems were somewhat neglected because the anthologies succeeded so well, yet in his lifetime they were praised for pure style and fine treatment.
britannica-1911-adam-william:
William Adam (1751-1839) was a British lawyer and politician. He was born in 1751, nephew of the architect Robert Adam. Edinburgh and Glasgow universities educated him. He passed at the Scottish bar in 1773. England drew him soon afterwards. He entered parliament in 1774 for a borough. In 1782 he joined the English bar. His practice there grew very considerable.

Whig politics shaped his public life. Adam supported Fox's policy throughout his career. He managed the impeachment of Warren Hastings. He defended Lord Melville at his impeachment too. In 1814 he became a Scottish baron of Exchequer. He then chief-commissioned the new jury court. That court tried civil causes until 1830. He died at Edinburgh in February 1839.
britannica-1911-adams-william:
William Adams (died 1620) was an English navigator. He was born at Gillingham near Chatham. At twelve he was apprenticed to the sea. The British navy and Barbary merchants employed him later. Dutch trade with India attracted him strongly. In 1598 he sailed as pilot major from the Texel. Five Rotterdam ships made the little fleet. Weather scattered them beyond the Magellan straits. His Charity reached Japan's Kiushiu in April 1600. Its crew was sick and dying on arrival.

Japan made him a resident adviser. Iyeyasu examined him at Osaka personally. His shipbuilding knowledge raised him in the shogun's esteem. An estate at Hemi rewarded his service. Permission to return home was refused for years. Adams married a Japanese woman and raised a family. He helped organize the English factory at Hirado.
britannica-1911-afzelius-adam:
Adam Afzelius, a Swedish botanist, is noted in a brief life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Larf in 1750, he first taught eastern tongues at Upsala. In 1785 he took a post showing plants to students there. From 1792 he spent some years on the west coast of Africa. In 1797 and 1798 he served at the Swedish mission in London.

Back home, Afzelius set up the Linnaean institute at Upsala in 1802. In 1812 he took the chair of materia medica at the school. He put out plant works and, in 1823, the life tale of Linnaeus. His kin won note too, one in the study of chemicals. A third brother rose as a famed teacher of medicine at Upsala.
britannica-1911-agram:
Agram is the capital of Croatia-Slavonia. Hungarians call it Zagrab, Croats call it Zagreb. The town is a royal free town of Hungary. It sits between the Save river's north bank. Mountains culminating in Sljeme rise behind it. Population approached fifty-eight thousand by 1900. The ban, or viceroy, has his seat there. The land's highest courts sit there too. Parliament meets in Agram for the kingdom.

Three districts divide the city. The Bishop's Town holds the archbishop's palace. Its late Gothic cathedral dates from the fifteenth century. The Upper Town holds the ban's palace. The Lower Town holds business, the university, and the academy. Ladislaus I founded Agram in 1094, the entry says. It became capital of Croatia-Slavonia in 1867.
britannica-1911-aikman-william:
Aikman, William, a British portrait-painter of 1682 to 1731, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Cairney in Forfarshire, he was meant by his father for the bar, the legal profession. He followed his own bent instead and studied under Sir John Medina, then Scotland's leading painter. In 1707 he set out for Italy.

Three years in Rome were followed by travel to Constantinople and Smyrna before he came home in 1712. In Edinburgh he painted portraits under the duke of Argyll's patronage. Moving to London in 1723 brought him many important commissions fast. His portrait of the poet Gay may have been his best work, and his truthful likenesses followed Sir Godfrey Kneller's style closely. Swift, Pope, Thomson, and Allan Ramsay counted among his friends.
britannica-1911-allan-sir-william:
Russia was where Sir William Allan (1782–1850) meant to make his fortune. London had failed him: study there led to no firm footing. Still, he showed his first picture there, A Gipsy Boy and Ass, at the Royal Academy in 1805, painted in Opie's manner. With scanty means he sailed for Russia that same year, only for bad weather to land his ship at Memel instead.

Edinburgh had given the Scottish painter his start. As a young pupil he entered the School of Design kept by the Board of Trustees for Arts and Manufactures. At the same table sat John Wilkie and the engraver John Burnet. Allan and Wilkie formed a friendship there that lasted all their lives.
britannica-1911-allen-william:
William Allen lived from 1532 to 1594 and was an English cardinal of the Roman church. The 1911 Britannica life starts at Rossall in Lancashire, his birth place. He went to Oriel College at Oxford in 1547 and rose fast there. By 1556 he was head of St Mary Hall and a proctor.

When Elizabeth came to the throne, his path changed at once. He lost his post for refusing the oath of supremacy. In time he fled to Louvain, where exiled English scholars had gathered. There he wrote tracts in defence of the old faith. Trips back home in secret put him at risk from the crown.
britannica-1911-anklam:
Anklam is a town of Germany in Prussian Pomerania. It stands on the Peene river. Stettin lies fifty-three miles south-east. The Stralsund railway serves the town. Its population in 1900 was 14,602. Fortifications were dismantled in 1762. They were never restored afterwards. The old walls still stand, though. Wars once made Anklam militarily important.

The Thirty Years' War battered the town severely. The Seven Years' War did the same. Fire and plague repeatedly ravaged it too. Its history is thus unusually eventful. No remarkable buildings survive, the entry says. Several quaint, picturesque houses remain instead. St Mary's church dates to the twelfth century. Its modern tower rises 335 feet. Iron foundries lead local industry. Sugar and soap factories also operate. The navigable Peene supports considerable trade. Shipbuilding occupies wharves along the river.
britannica-1911-annam:
Annam is a country of south-eastern Asia. It now forms a French protectorate. The Indo-China peninsula holds it. Tongking bounds it on the north. The China Sea washes its east. Cochin-China lies to the south-west. Cambodia and Laos border the west. The territory forms a sinuous strip. It stretches 750 to 800 miles long. Its area is about 52,000 square miles.

Population is estimated at about 6,124,000. Plateaus and wooded mountains dominate the country. They run north and south throughout. A narrow coastal plain edges the mountains. That plain varies from twelve to fifty miles wide. Short valleys cut the ranges transversely. Rivers there run dry in summer. Winter turns them torrential. Tourane bay affords the chief harbour. The rainy season begins in September. It lasts three or four months. The long entry covers people, products, and administration.
britannica-1911-archer-william:
William Archer (1856– ) is an English critic. He was born at Perth in September 1856. Edinburgh University educated him. He became a leader-writer in 1875. The Edinburgh Evening News employed him then. A year in Australia interrupted his career. He returned to Edinburgh afterwards. In 1879 he became the London Figaro's dramatic critic. The World took him in 1884.

He soon held a prominent literary place. Introducing Ibsen to England was his great service. He translated The Pillars of Society himself. The Gaiety Theatre produced it in 1880. A Doll's House followed in his translation in 1889. The Master Builder and Peer Gynt followed too. He edited Ibsen's Prose Dramas in five volumes. His own critical works are numerous. English Dramatists of To-day appeared in 1882. The Theatrical World collected his notices yearly.
britannica-1911-assam:
Assam is the subject of a region article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Assam was a former province of British India on the northeast border of Bengal. In 1905 it was joined with Eastern Bengal. Its area was over fifty six thousand square miles. By 1901 its people numbered over six million. Bhutan and Tibet lay beyond it to the north, and Burma to the east.

The article maps its bounds on each side in close detail. It then splits the land into three natural parts. One part is the Brahmaputra valley, a flat plain some four hundred fifty miles long. A second part is the Surma valley. Between them lie hill ranges named for the tribes who live in them. Peaks in those ranges rise from about forty six hundred feet to near ten thousand feet. Readers get a clear lay of a frontier land.
britannica-1911-bainbridge-william:
Bainbridge, William (1774-1833), was a commodore in the United States navy. He was born at Princeton, New Jersey. At fourteen he went to sea in merchant ships. He soon commanded a trading schooner. French and British cruisers harassed such neutral traders.

The United States navy formed in 1798. Bainbridge joined its officer corps at once. He cruised against the French in the brig Norfolk. He also carried tribute money to the dey of Algiers. He performed that hated duty punctually. Later he fought the Barbary states themselves. His ship Philadelphia ran aground off Tunis. He spent a time as a prisoner there. After release he returned to merchant work. He needed to repair the money loss from captivity.
britannica-1911-bairam:
Bairam is a Perso-Turkish word meaning festival. Turkish use applies it to two chief festivals of Islam. The first is the Lesser Festival. Turks also call it the Sugar Bairam. Arabic speakers call it the Festival of Fast-breaking. It follows the fasting month of Ramadan.

That feast fills the first three days of Shawwal. Officials hold receptions then. Friends visit and give presents. New clothes are worn. Graves of relatives are visited. The second feast is the Greater Festival, or Sacrifice Bairam. It falls late in the pilgrimage month. Pilgrims at Mina slay an animal there. The rite recalls Ishmael's ransom with a ram. Muslims everywhere copy the sacrifice if they can. Both feasts follow the moon. They drift through the solar year.
britannica-1911-balaam:
Balaam was a prophet in the Bible. He was son of Beor. A Gentile seer is his standing here. Israel met him in Moab's plains. That meeting came late in the wandering. Moses still lived at that point. Jordan's crossing lay just ahead.

Israel had beaten two eastern kings. Sihon and Og had fallen already. Balak of Moab grew alarmed at that. He sent for Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam hesitated before coming at all. When he sought to curse, God compelled blessing. Seven oracular poems frame the tale. Numbers chapters twenty-two to twenty-five hold it. The entry weighs the story's sources closely. Two old documents, J and E, underlie it. Their exact shares remain uncertain. Later Old Testament references disagree somewhat. Ancient traditions in varied forms explain that.
britannica-1911-balfe-michael-william:
Michael William Balfe (1808–1870) was an Irish composer, born at Dublin on 15 May 1808. His father, a dancing master, was almost his only teacher, along with the musician C. E. Horn. The boy played violin for his father's classes and wrote a polacca at the age of seven.

After his father died in 1823, Balfe joined the Drury Lane orchestra and turned to opera singing, though his first try at Norwich failed. Taken to Rome in 1825, he wrote his first stage work, a ballet. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his years in Italy, singing and writing operas, and his marriage to the Hungarian singer Luisa Roser.
britannica-1911-ballantine-william:
William Ballantine (1812–1887) was an English serjeant-at-law, born in London on 3 January 1812, the son of a police magistrate. Schooled at St Paul's, he was called to the bar in 1834. Early mixing in stage and literary circles, plus a sharp mind and a pushing nature, soon built him a large practice, above all in criminal cases.

Ballantine became known as a feared cross-examiner. The 1911 Britannica entry names the three great cases of his career. He prosecuted the murderer Franz Müller in 1864. He defended the Tichborne claimant in 1871. He defended the gaekwar of Baroda in 1875, for a fee among the largest ever known. He died poor at Margate in 1887.
britannica-1911-balsam:
Balsam, in the strict sense used here, is a resin or oleo-resin that holds benzoic acid or cinnamic acid, or both. Such balsams form a clear class, alike in make-up, traits, and uses. The word came through Latin and French forms that also gave English the word balm.

Four trade kinds fill the 1911 Britannica entry. Balsam of Peru, a thick, dark, sweet-smelling resin from a tall tree in San Salvador, serves perfumery. Balsam of Tolu, thicker still, goes into cough syrups and lozenges as well as scent. Liquid storax comes from a tree of Asia Minor. Each kind gets its source, look, and chief use in turn.
britannica-1911-bam:
Bam is a town of Persia in the province of Kerman, 115 miles south-east of the city of Kerman. It stands 3,600 feet up, on both banks of the river Bam, and serves as capital of the Bam-Narmashir district. Its population was about 13,000.

Wide groves of date palms and gardens surround the town. Outside it stands a famous citadel with walls 40 feet high, counted even at the start of the 19th century as the strongest fortified place in Persia. The 1911 Britannica entry explains that strength: the Afghans took Bam in 1719 and were not finally driven out until 1801. Post and telegraph offices had opened there by 1903.
britannica-1911-bantam:
Bantam is the subject of a region entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was the westernmost residency of the island of Java in the Dutch East Indies. The Strait of Sunda bounds it on the west and the Java Sea on the north. Batavia and Preanger lay to the east, with the Indian Ocean to the south.

The entry gives its population in eighteen ninety seven, split by groups. Most natives were Sundanese, except in the north where they were Javanese. The coast is low and often marshy, the text notes. Islands in the strait and along the coast also fall within the residency.
britannica-1911-barclay-william:
William Barclay (1546–1608) was a Scottish jurist, born in Aberdeenshire in 1546 and educated at Aberdeen University. He went to France in 1573 and studied law under Cujas at Bourges, taking his doctor's degree there. Charles III, duke of Lorraine, made him professor of civil law at the new university of Pont-à-Mousson, plus counsellor of state.

Jesuit hostility drove him out in 1603, after he fought their bid to draw his son John into their society. In England, King James offered him rich preferment if he would join the Church of England; he refused and returned to France as professor at Angers, where he died. The 1911 Britannica entry names his chief works: a defence of kings' rights against Buchanan and others, and a tract against the pope's claim to temporal power.
britannica-1911-barnes-william:
William Barnes (1800–1886), the Dorset poet, was born on 22 February 1800 at Rushay, near Pentridge in Dorset, son of a farmer and of Grace Scott. A delicate child of bookish, retiring temper, he was picked out at Sturminster Newton school as its clever boy and taken as a solicitor's pupil.

Barnes worked with the village parson at classics and learned music from the organist, then moved to Dorchester in 1818 for further office work and evening study. He took up wood-engraving, and the pay for blocks for a book of walks about Dorchester let him print his first book, Orra, a Lapland Tale, in 1822. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, follows his school at Mere, his marriage, and his life as the poet of Dorset speech.
britannica-1911-bates-william:
William Bates (1625–1699), an English nonconformist divine born in London, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied at Emmanuel College and then King's College, Cambridge. A Presbyterian in belief, he held the rich living of St Dunstan's-in-the-West in London. He sat on the board that met at the Savoy to review the public liturgy, and he helped draw up the faults found in the Book of Common Prayer.

Favour at court did not keep Bates in place. Charles II made him a chaplain and offered him a deanery, yet in 1662 Bates came out as one of the 2000 ministers cast out for refusing the new rules. A mild man, he worked with other moderate men for a broad church settlement, but the bishops would not yield. On the accession of William and Mary he spoke for the dissenters. He died at Hackney in 1699.
britannica-1911-batten-sir-william:
Sir William Batten (active 1626–1667), a British sailor and son of a master in the royal navy, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He first appears taking out letters of marque in 1626. In 1638 he gained the post of surveyor to the navy, most likely by purchase. In 1642 he became second in command under the earl of Warwick, the parliament admiral who took the fleet from the king.

Civil war split Batten's service. His ships bombarded Scarborough when Queen Henrietta Maria landed there. He stayed a firm man for parliament to the first war's end. In 1648 he joined the fleet party that went over to the prince of Wales in Holland. Knighted there, he was then cast ashore by his new friends and came home. At the Restoration he became surveyor again and sat for Rochester. Pepys, whose diary often names him, worked with him daily.
britannica-1911-battering-ram:
Battering-ram, in Latin aries, a ram, was a war engine used before cannon to beat down the walls of besieged towns, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. It was a long, heavy beam of timber, tipped with iron shaped somewhat like a ram's head. In its simplest form men carried the beam in their hands. They drove it at the wall by main force until the stones gave way.

Growth in size brought new gear. The improved ram could run to 120 feet long. It hung by ropes from a beam across two posts, roofed by a penthouse to shield its crew. It often stood on wheels, and a hundred men at a time might work it in relays. No wall, the entry says, could stand its steady blows for long. Defenders fought it with dropped stones, hooks to seize its head, and mines under its shed.
britannica-1911-baxter-william:
William Baxter (1650–1723), a British antiquarian, critic, and grammarian, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a nephew of Richard Baxter, the Puritan divine. Born at Llanllugan in Montgomeryshire, he went to Harrow school at eighteen unable to read, and able to speak no language but Welsh. His rise from that start is the entry's wonder: about ten years later he published a Latin grammar. For most of his life he was a schoolmaster, ending as headmaster of the Mercers' school in London, and he died in May 1723.

Great learning fills the second half. Baxter was a skilled linguist whose knowledge the entry calls very great indeed. His works include De Analogia, an advanced Latin grammar, and an edition of Anacreon with odes of Sappho. His Horace was famed for its abuse of the scholar Bentley.
britannica-1911-bazalgette-sir-joseph-wi:
Sir Joseph William Bazalgette (1819–1891) was an English engineer born at Enfield. Articled at seventeen, he soon set up a sound practice of his own. His name rests chiefly on two great London works: the main drainage system and the Thames embankment.

As chief engineer to the Metropolitan Board of Works from 1855, Bazalgette built eighty-three miles of large intercepting sewers, opened in 1865 at a cost of £4,600,000. The network drained over a hundred square miles and could handle 420 million gallons a day. He also planned bridges at Putney and Battersea and the Woolwich steam ferry before his death in 1891.
britannica-1911-beaver-dam:
Beaver Dam, a city of Dodge county in Wisconsin, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the south east of the state, sixty three miles north west of Milwaukee. The city stands on Beaver Lake, which runs nine miles long and three miles wide. Its people grew from 4222 in 1890 to 6758 in 1910, most of German descent.

A rail line serves the city, which draws summer guests and holds a public library. Wayland Academy, a Baptist school from 1855 tied to the university of Chicago, sits there. Fine farm land rings the town, and lake power drives its works. Those works turn out woollen and cotton goods, iron wares, engines, farm tools, stoves, and beer. First settlement came at about 1841.
britannica-1911-beckford-william:
