William Beckford, an English author who lived from 1760 to 1844, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a lord mayor of London famed for a bold speech to the king. At the age of eleven the boy came into a princely fortune. He wed in 1783, and after his wife's death he roamed Spain and Portugal.

His book of letters from that tour ranks with his best work. At Fonthill Abbey he built a vast house at a cost the entry puts at a huge sum. One of its towers fell in ruins not long after he sold the place. His chief fame rests on Vathek, a tale of the East first written in French. He also bought the great stock of books left by Gibbon.
britannica-1911-bedell-william:
William Bedell is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Bedell was an Anglican churchman, born in Essex in 1571. He was educated at Cambridge and became a fellow of Emmanuel in 1593. In 1607 he went to Venice as chaplain to the English ambassador.

Four years in Venice made his name as a scholar and theologian. He translated the Book of Common Prayer into Italian there. He also formed a close friendship with the reformer Paolo Sarpi. Back in England he held a rectory near Bury St Edmunds for twelve years. In 1627 he became provost of Trinity College, Dublin. Two years later he was made bishop of Kilmore and Ardagh. There he set himself to reform the abuses of his diocese. He encouraged the use of the Irish language and took up parish duties himself.
britannica-1911-bell-alexander-graham:
Alexander Graham Bell (born 1847) was an American inventor and physicist, born at Edinburgh in Scotland. He studied at the universities of Edinburgh and London, then moved with his father to Canada in 1870. Two years later he became professor of vocal physiology at Boston University.

In 1876 Bell showed a device that sent sound by electricity, the seed of the modern telephone as trade soon took it up. He also devised the photophone, which carried sound on a beam of light, and worked on phonographic gear. Later he turned to the problem of flight by machine, and wrote many papers, one on a deaf variety in the human race.
britannica-1911-bellenden-william:
William Bellenden was a Scottish classical scholar of whom almost nothing personal is known. He lived under James I of England, who made him master of requests and is said to have funded his life at Paris. There Bellenden became a professor at the university and an advocate in the parliament, dying some time after 1625.

His fame rests on books built out of Cicero. Ciceronis Princeps of 1608 gathers all Cicero’s remarks on kingship, ordered by topic, and Ciceronis Consul of 1612 does the same for consuls and the senate. De Statu Prisci Orbis outlines general history, and his vast De Tribus Luminibus Romanorum fed, some charged by theft, into Middleton’s Life of Cicero.
britannica-1911-bellingham:
Bellingham is a city of Whatcom county, Washington, on the east side of Bellingham Bay, ninety-six miles north of Seattle. It held 11,062 people in 1900 and 24,298 by 1910, over some twenty-three square miles. Four railways meet there, one ending in the town and reaching toward the Mount Baker goldfields.

Lake Whatcom, thirteen miles long, feeds the city’s water by gravity through a system that cost a million dollars. Two Carnegie libraries, the court-house and the state’s largest normal college stand among its chief buildings. Its fine harbour, nearest of any American port to Alaska’s markets, makes Bellingham a busy shipping centre built from two older towns in 1903.
britannica-1911-bentinck-lord-william:
Lord William Bentinck (1774–1839) was governor-general of India, second son of the third duke of Portland. He entered the army, rose to lieutenant-colonel and stood at Marengo. Sent out as governor of Madras in 1803, he quarrelled with the chief justice and council, and the Vellore sepoy mutiny of 1807 brought his recall.

Twenty years later Bentinck returned as governor-general, serving from 1827 to 1835. His rule brought many reforms: the Thugs were suppressed, suttee was abolished, and English was made the base of education in India, the step behind Macaulay’s famous minute. The entry calls his administration peaceful, progressive and successful. He died at Paris in June 1839.
britannica-1911-berkeley-sir-william:
Sir William Berkeley (about 1608–1677) was a British colonial governor in America, youngest son of Sir Maurice Berkeley of the London Company. Oxford graduated him in 1629, and royal favour made him a gentleman of the privy chamber under Charles I. He even tried the stage, writing a tragi-comedy, The Lost Lady, in 1638.

Named governor of Virginia in 1641, Berkeley proved popular with most colonists, though his religious intolerance drove out the Puritan minority. Loyal through the Civil War, he retired in 1652 when a parliamentary fleet arrived, then returned as governor in 1660. His later rule ended in recall in 1677 after Bacon’s rebellion shook the colony; he died at Twickenham that July. The entry also credits his Discourse and View of Virginia of 1663.
britannica-1911-bimlipatam:
Bimlipatam is a town of British India in the Vizagapatam district of Madras. It stands on the sea coast, 18 miles north-east of Vizagapatam town. Its population in 1901 was 10,212. It was once a Dutch factory, or trading post, in earlier colonial days. By 1911 it was the principal port of its district. Its anchorage is an open roadstead, partly sheltered by headlands. A lighthouse stands at Santapalli nearby.

Nearly half the town's sea-borne trade runs to foreign countries, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Oil-seeds, hides, and jute head the list of exports. The entry is a short port gazetteer note of a few lines. It gives no history beyond the Dutch factory past. No industries, temples, or officials are named in the text. The roadstead, the lighthouse, and the export list carry the whole account of the place.
britannica-1911-binney-edward-william:
Edward William Binney (1812–1881) was an English geologist, born at Morton in Nottinghamshire. He trained as a solicitor at Chesterfield and settled at Manchester in 1836. He soon left legal practice for geology as his chief pursuit. In 1838 he helped found the Manchester Geological Society. He served it as secretary, then twice as president. He also led the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society in turn.

His field was the Carboniferous and Permian rocks of northern England. He studied Lancashire's drift deposits and the ground around Manchester with care. On the Coal Measures he became a recognized authority, the 1911 Britannica entry says. His work on fossil plant structure ran from 1868 to 1875 as a society monograph. His large fossil collection went to Owens College. He became a fellow of the Royal Society in 1856. He died at Manchester in December 1881.
britannica-1911-black-adam:
Adam Black (1784–1874) was a Scottish publisher and founder of the firm of A. & C. Black in Edinburgh. Born in Edinburgh, the son of a builder, he trained in the bookselling trade and set up on his own in 1808. His nephew Charles joined him in business a few years later.

Two deals shaped the firm, as the entry tells it. Black and friends bought the copyright of the Encyclopaedia Britannica in 1827, and in 1851 the firm paid £27,000 for the Waverley Novels. Black was twice lord provost of Edinburgh and sat in parliament for the city from 1856 to 1865. He retired in 1865, and his sons later moved the business to London.
britannica-1911-blackstone-sir-william:
Sir William Blackstone (1723–1780) was an English judge and law teacher whose Commentaries shaped how English law was understood. Born in London and orphaned young, he was raised by his uncle, schooled at Charterhouse, and sent to Pembroke College, Oxford, at fifteen. He joined the Middle Temple in 1741 and was called to the bar in 1746.

At Oxford he became a fellow of All Souls, helped run the college, and from 1753 gave lectures on the laws of England, the first of their kind. Those lectures grew into his famous Commentaries. The closing pages judge the book's huge sway over public feeling about the constitution, even where its hold as a court authority had faded.
britannica-1911-blackwood-william:
William Blackwood (1776–1834) was a Scottish publisher who founded William Blackwood and Sons and the magazine that bore his name. Born to humble parents in Edinburgh, he was apprenticed to booksellers at fourteen and worked in Edinburgh, Glasgow, and London. In 1804 he opened his own shop for old and rare books.

He moved to Princes Street in 1816 and drifted into publishing for himself. In April 1817 he launched the Edinburgh Monthly Magazine, soon renamed Blackwood's, which became the voice of the Scottish Tories and drew many able writers. After his death his sons ran the firm, and his younger brother John later led it. George Eliot's first stories appeared in the magazine.
britannica-1911-blades-william:
William Blades (1824–1890) was an English printer who became a leading student of early English printing. Born at Clapham in London, he was apprenticed at fourteen to his father's printing firm and later taken into partnership. The business became known as Blades, East and Blades.

His fame rests on close study of the books printed by Caxton. In his Life and Typography of William Caxton (1861–1863) he traced each sort of type from first use to worn-out end and sorted some 450 Caxton volumes in date order. He helped plan the Caxton celebration of 1877, backed the founding of the Library Association, and wrote the popular Enemies of Books in 1881.
britannica-1911-bloemaert-abraham:
Abraham Bloemaert, who lived from 1564 to 1651, was a Dutch painter and engraver born at Gorinchem. The 1911 Britannica article says his father was an architect. He learned first from Gerrit Splinter and Joos de Beer at Utrecht. He then spent three years in Paris under several masters. Back home, he took more training from Hieronymus Francken. In 1591 he went to Amsterdam.

Four years later Bloemaert settled for good at Utrecht. There he became dean of the Guild of Saint Luke. The article rates his colour above his drawing. He was a most fertile hand, turning out works of history and myth, landscapes, still life, beasts, and flowers. His pupils were many. Chief among them were his four sons, all of whom won fame with brush or needle, and the two Honthorsts.
britannica-1911-blomfield-sir-arthur-wil:
Sir Arthur William Blomfield, an English architect, is set out in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1829, he was a son of a bishop of London. He was schooled at Rugby and at Trinity College, Cambridge. Then he trained in the office of a working architect. In time he built a large practice of his own.

Blomfield led the Architectural Association as its head in 1861. He joined the royal body of architects as fellow, then vice head. In 1887 he became architect to the Bank of England. He drew the bank's law courts branch in Fleet Street. Knighted in 1889, he died ten years later in 1899. His church work at St Saviour's, Southwark, shows his revived Gothic hand.
britannica-1911-blount-william:
William Blount, an American politician who lived from 1749 to 1800, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Bertie county, North Carolina, in March 1749, he sat in the Continental Congress in the 1780s. He took part in the Philadelphia convention of 1787 and in the convention that ratified the Federal constitution in 1789.

From 1790 to 1796 Blount governed the Territory South of the Ohio River by appointment of President Washington. He was also superintendent of Indian affairs there. In 1791 he laid out Knoxville as the seat of government. He presided over the Tennessee constitutional convention of 1796. On statehood he became one of Tennessee's first senators. In 1797 his link to a scheme called Blount's Conspiracy became known. The plan aimed to seize Florida and Louisiana from Spain for Britain, using frontiersmen, Indians, and an English force.
britannica-1911-bonham:
Bonham is a town in north-east Texas and the county seat of Fannin county, about 14 miles south of the Red River and 70 miles north of Dallas. Its people numbered 3361 in 1890, 5042 in 1900, and 4844 in 1910. Two railway lines served it.

Carlton College, a Christian women's college founded in 1867, stood in the town, and its high school is praised as one of the best in the state. Bonham shipped the goods of a wide farm country growing cotton, corn, and fruit and raising livestock. Cotton gins, a cotton mill, flour mills, and railway shops are listed. The town honours J. B. Bonham, killed at the Alamo, was first settled in 1836, and was incorporated in 1850.
britannica-1911-booth-william:
William Booth (born 1829) was the founder and general of the Salvation Army. Born at Nottingham, he took a strong religious turn at fifteen under Wesleyan Methodists and became a local preacher. In London from 1849, his love of open-air preaching split him from the Wesleyans, by his own account.

Ordained in the Methodist New Connexion, he left that body too in 1861 when it would not use him as a travelling evangelist. With his wife Catherine, married in 1855, he preached in Cornwall, Cardiff, and Walsall, where a Hallelujah band of converted wrongdoers first formed. In London from 1864 he built a mission that took new names in turn, becoming the Salvation Army in 1878. Its methods, from street meetings to rescue work, fill the entry's second half.
britannica-1911-borden-sir-frederick-wil: Sir Frederick William Borden (born 1847) was a Canadian doctor turned Liberal minister. He was born at Cornwallis, Nova Scotia, on 14 May 1847. He studied at King's College, Windsor, and at Harvard. For some years he practised medicine at Canning. In 1874 he entered parliament as Liberal member for King's county. In 1896 he became minister of militia and defence. The entry is brief, giving schooling, medical years, first election, and cabinet post.
britannica-1911-bouguereau-adolphe-willi:
Adolphe William Bouguereau (1825–1905) was a French academic painter. He was born at La Rochelle. He trained at the École des Beaux-Arts from 1843 to 1850. In 1850 he shared the Grand Prix de Rome with Baudry. The set subject was Zenobia on the banks of the Araxes. Frescoes at Pompeii and Herculaneum shaped his Idyll of 1853.

Back in Paris he decorated grand houses. He showed at the Salon from 1847. His Martyr's Triumph went to the Luxembourg after the 1855 exhibition. It shows the body of St Cecilia borne to the catacombs. The state set him to paint the emperor's visit to flood sufferers at Tarascon. A first prize medal came in 1857. Wax-painted panels for the Bartholomy mansion are listed among his much-discussed works.
britannica-1911-brixham:
Brixham is a seaport and market town in Devonshire, England, 33 miles south of Exeter on a Great Western branch line, in the Torquay parliamentary division. Its urban district held 8092 people in 1901. The town is built without regular plan on cliffs south of Torbay, and a breakwater shelters its harbour.

Fishing rules its work: Brixham is headquarters of the Devonshire sea fisheries, with a large coasting trade beside it, plus shipbuilding and making of ropes, paint and sails. Bathing draws visitors as a seaside resort. St Mary's, the old parish church, holds a fine 14th-century font, and a boys' home trains orphans of British seamen for the merchant service. A statue marks the landing of William of Orange here in 1688. Nearby Brixham Cave, or Windmill Hill Cavern, sealed until found by chance in 1858, was dug out under Dr Hugh Falconer for its fossil bones.
britannica-1911-broome-william:
William Broome (1689–1745) was an English scholar and poet, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica links his name with Pope. He was the son of a farmer, born at Haslington in Cheshire. He was baptized there on the third of May 1689. He was educated at Eton, where he became captain of the school.

From Eton Broome went to St John’s College, Cambridge, for his degree. In 1712 he worked with two partners on a version of the Iliad. That version was made from the French rendering of Madame Dacier. Verses of his own appeared the same year in a miscellany. He was then presented to Pope, who was at work on his own Iliad. Pope asked him to digest the notes of Eustathius on Homer. Broome did that task to the full pleasure of Pope, and refused any payment for it.
britannica-1911-browne-william:
William Browne (1591–1643) was an English pastoral poet born at Tavistock in Devonshire in 1591, of a branch of the Browne family of Betchworth Castle, Surrey. Schooled at his home town's grammar school, he is said to have gone to Oxford about 1603, then after a short stay at Clifford's Inn entered the Inner Temple in 1611. Poetry came early and thick.

An elegy on the death of Henry, prince of Wales. The first book of Britannia's Pastorals both appeared in 1613, the Shepherd's Pipe with eclogues by other poets in 1614. The second book of the Pastorals in 1616, dedicated to William Herbert, earl of Pembroke, at whose seat Wilton Browne lived for a time. In 1624 he returned to Oxford as tutor to Robert Dormer, later earl of Carnarvon, taking his master's degree that November. Nearly all his verse dates from before his marriage in 1628, a point George Wither's Shepherd's Hunting already teased him for in 1613-1614.
britannica-1911-buckingham:
Buckingham is a market town in Buckinghamshire, England. It is the county town of that shire. It lies 61 miles north-west of London. A branch railway of the London & North-Western serves it. Its population in 1901 was 3152. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town and its past. The river Ouse loops around it on three sides.

The church of St Peter and St Paul stands on the old castle site. It dates from the 18th century. Sir Gilbert Scott, a local man, restored it. The grammar school was founded by Edward VI. It keeps windows and a Norman door from older buildings. Nearby stands Stowe, a great mansion in fine gardens. It was the seat of the dukes of Buckingham until 1889. The town trades in farm goods. It makes condensed milk and artificial manure. Pillow-lace making survives as an old industry. The entry recalls Edward the Elder's forts there in 918.
britannica-1911-buckland-william:
William Buckland (1784–1856) was an English divine and geologist. This 1911 Britannica biography follows his career at Oxford. He was born at Axminster on 12 March 1784. He was schooled at Tiverton and at Winchester. In 1801 he won a scholarship to Corpus Christi College, Oxford. He took his degree in 1804 and became a fellow in 1809. He also entered holy orders that year.

From boyhood Buckland loved natural science. He studied the strata of Britain on foot. He noted their order and their fossil remains. In 1813 he became reader in mineralogy at Oxford. His lectures drew such crowds that a new readership followed. In 1819 a chair of geology was founded for him. He was president of the Geological Society twice. He also held a canonry at Christ Church. The entry treats his church posts and his science together.
britannica-1911-buckram:
Buckram is a stiff cloth used in clothing and books. This short 1911 Britannica entry traces the word and the fabric. The word appears in many European tongues. The French form is bouqueran, and the Italian is bucherame. Its root is unknown, the entry says. In early use the name meant a fine linen or cotton cloth.

Today the word means a much coarser fabric. It is linen or cotton stiffened with glue. Tailors use it for linings of clothes. Bookbinders use it in covering books. The entry ends with a famous stage phrase. Falstaff speaks of “men in buckram” in Shakespeare's Henry IV. That line has become a proverb for imaginary persons. The whole notice is a few lines long. It gives the word's forms, its old and new senses, and its literary echo.
britannica-1911-burke-william:
William Burke, an Irish criminal who lived from 1792 to 1829, is the subject of a grim 1911 Britannica article. He was born in Ireland and tried his hand at many trades there. About 1817 he went to Scotland as a navvy. By 1827 he was living in an Edinburgh lodging-house kept by William Hare.

Late that year, one of Hare's lodgers died. The dead man was an old army pensioner. It was the age of the body-snatchers, and corpses fetched ready money. The two men sold the body to Dr Robert Knox, a leading Edinburgh anatomist. The price and the ease of the sale struck Hare as a way to make a living. Burke fell in with the plan at once. The article opens the tale of crimes that made both names a byword for murder for gain.
britannica-1911-carey-william:
William Carey (1761–1834) was an English Oriental scholar and missionary. He is called the pioneer of modern missionary enterprise. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born at Paulerspury, Northamptonshire, on 17 August 1761. As a youth he worked as a shoemaker. He joined the Baptists at about twenty-one. He gave much time to village preaching. In 1787 he became pastor of a Baptist church in Leicester.

Carey's energy helped form the Baptist Missionary Society. He was among the first of its men to go abroad. In Bengal in 1793 he lost all his property in the Hugli river. An indigo factory post at Malda kept the work alive. There he began translating the Bible into Bengali. In 1799 he moved to Serampore and built a press. From 1801 he taught Oriental languages at Fort William college. His grammars and dictionaries covered many Indian tongues. A fire destroyed his great Sanskrit dictionary manuscript.
britannica-1911-carleton-william:
William Carleton (1794–1869) was an Irish novelist. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his life and background. He was born at Prillisk, in county Tyrone, on 4 March 1794. His father was a tenant farmer with fourteen children. The family lived on as many acres of land. Carleton's early life matched the scenes he later drew. His novels picture that world with power and truth.

His father had an extraordinary memory for folklore. His mother was famed in the district for her singing voice. The character of Honor, in Fardorougha, was drawn from her. Carleton's schooling was of the humblest kind. He attended hedge-schools as the family moved between farms. One such school is pictured in his sketch “The Hedge School.” A curate named Keenan taught him classics at Donagh. He studied there from 1814 to 1816. The article follows his rise as a writer from there.
britannica-1911-carstares-william:
William Carstares (1649–1715) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Scottish clergyman born at Cathcart, near Glasgow, the son of a minister of the extreme Covenanting party. He studied at Edinburgh and then at Utrecht, where he began a lifelong friendship with the prince of Orange. He carried secret messages between the disaffected in Scotland and Holland, work that made the government watch him.

On his return to England late in 1674 he was sent to the Tower, then moved to Edinburgh Castle, and he stayed a prisoner until August 1679. Later he served a Nonconformist congregation at Cheshunt. In 1683 he was caught up in the Rye House Plot and examined before the Scottish Council. The thumb screw was applied, yet he said nothing until promised that his admissions would not be used in evidence.
britannica-1911-cartwright-william:
William Cartwright (1611–1643) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English dramatist and divine. He was born at Northway in Gloucestershire. His father was a gentleman reduced to keeping an inn. Cartwright was educated at Cirencester and at Westminster school. He then went to Christ Church, Oxford. He took his master's degree in 1635. Contemporaries praised him as the most florid preacher in the university.

Cartwright counted himself a “son” of Ben Jonson. He stood high in favour with his peers. Henry Lawes set some of his songs to music. The king wore mourning on the day of his funeral. The entry judges his plays, apart from The Ordinary, as fantastic in plot and stiff in treatment. His Royal Slave was performed by Christ Church students before the king and queen in 1636. He died in November 1643.
britannica-1911-caxton-william:
William Caxton was the first English printer, who lived from about fourteen twenty-two to fourteen ninety-one. He was born in the Weald of Kent. At about age sixteen he was bound to a rich silk trader of London. When that man died, the youth was sent to Bruges to end his term.

At Bruges he rose to head the group of English traders in the Low Lands. He served on talks to renew the wool trade pact with Burgundy. In time he joined the house of the duchess Margaret. His work on a French tale of Troy led him toward print. The entry tracks that shift in full.
britannica-1911-ceram:
Ceram, an island of the Dutch East Indies in the Molucca group, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It runs a bit over two hundred miles long and near fifty miles wide. Its area, with near islets, is 6,621 square miles. Two parts, Great and Little Ceram, are joined by a narrow neck of land.

Hills near the north coast rise to near 2,600 feet and slope steep to the shore. In the south a mass of peaks nears 5,000 feet. Rain is very heavy, at 121 inches a year on the south coast. Rivers can be sailed just a few miles in the wet season. Thick woods fill much of the inner land, and quakes are not rare.
britannica-1911-cheltenham:
Cheltenham is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a borough of Gloucestershire, England, 109 miles west by north of London by rail. Its population in 1901 was 49,439. The town sits in the valley of the Chelt, a small tributary of the Severn, under the Cotteswold Hills. It is in high repute as a health resort. Mineral springs were found by accident in 1716.

The Montpellier and Pittville springs supply handsome pump rooms in public gardens. The Montpellier waters are sulphated and act on the liver. The alkaline saline waters of Pittville answer diseases from excess of uric acid. The town is wholly modern in look, with a broad, tree lined Promenade. It is famous as a centre of schools. Cheltenham College dates from 1842 and the Ladies' College from 1854. The entry presents a spa town whose second industry is education.
britannica-1911-chesham:
Chesham is a market town in Buckinghamshire, England, 26 miles west-north-west of London, reached by the Metropolitan railway. Its urban district counted 7,245 people in 1901, and the town lies in the narrow valley of the river Chess. Low wooded hills flank the valley closely on both sides. The church of St Mary is cruciform and mainly Perpendicular, with old frescoes and many monuments preserved inside it.

Beech grown around the town is made into dairy utensils, chairs and malt shovels, and shoemaking is also carried on. At Waterside hamlet, next to the town, flour mills and duck farms work by the river. Wide watercress beds, for which the Chess is noted, spread there as well. The same river is also known for its trout fishing, the entry adds.
britannica-1911-chidambaram:
Chidambaram, or Chedumbrum, is a town of British India in the South Arcot district of Madras, seven miles from the coast and 151 miles south of Madras by rail. Its people numbered 19,909 in 1901, and its pagodas are the oldest in the south of India. Parts of them are called gems of art. The town is thought to mark the northern frontier of the ancient Chola kingdom.

The principal temple is sacred to Siva and draws upwards of 60,000 pilgrims every December. A tale links its rebuilding to a leper emperor cured by bathing in the temple tank. Its hall of a thousand pillars in fact has 984, each a block of solid granite, and the main temple roof is of copper gilt. Three hundred high caste Brahmins live with their families inside the enclosure.
britannica-1911-childs-george-william:
Childs, George William (1829–1894) was an American publisher, born in Baltimore, Maryland, on 12 May 1829 and educated in the public schools. After a brief term in the navy he became a clerk in a Philadelphia book shop in 1843. There in 1847 he set up his own book shop, and two years later he organised the publishing house of Childs and Peterson. He died at Philadelphia on 3 February 1894.

In 1864, with Anthony J Drexel, he bought the Public Ledger, then a little known newspaper, and changed its policy and methods wholly. Under him it became one of the most influential journals in the country. The entry stresses his public spirit and giving, from memorial windows in Westminster Abbey to a Shakespeare fountain at Stratford-on-Avon. With Drexel he also founded a home for Union printers at Colorado Springs in 1892.
britannica-1911-chillingworth-william:
Chillingworth, William (1602–1644) was an English divine and controversialist, born at Oxford in October 1602 and made a fellow of Trinity College there in 1628. He had a name as a skilful disputant, excelled in mathematics and wrote verses. A Jesuit named John Fisher converted him to Rome, and he went to the Jesuit college at Douai. His godfather Laud urged a fair inquiry, and he left Douai in 1631 and returned to Oxford.

On grounds of Scripture and reason he declared for Protestantism, though scruples over the Thirty-nine Articles long kept him from orders. His chief work, The Religion of Protestants a Safe Way to Salvation, appeared in 1637 in defence of Dr Potter against the Jesuit Edward Knott. It upholds the sole authority of the Bible and the free right of conscience to interpret it. A zealous Royalist, he was taken prisoner at Arundel Castle and died at Chichester in January 1644.
britannica-1911-chippenham:
Chippenham is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a market town and borough in Wiltshire, England, west of London on the Great Western line. The entry gives its count of people in nineteen hundred one and its small area. A mayor, aldermen, and councillors ran the town.

Inside, readers find the town in a hollow by the Upper Avon, crossed by a stone bridge of many arches. Saint Andrew's church, first built in Norman times, was enlarged in later styles. A paved path built by Maud Heath is also described. The entry notes grain and cheese markets and local trades in cloth, churns, and other goods.
britannica-1911-claflin-horace-brigham:
Claflin, Horace Brigham (1811–1885) was an American merchant, born in Milford, Massachusetts, on 18 December 1811 and educated at Milford Academy. He clerked in his father's store, then succeeded to that business in 1831 with his brother Aaron and his brother-in-law Samuel Daniels. A branch store opened at Worcester in 1832, and Claflin and Daniels soon held sole control of it, dealing only in dry goods. In 1843 he removed to New York City.

There he joined Bulkley and Claflin, wholesale dry goods merchants, and reorganised firms took his name in 1851 and 1864. Under his management sales for a time after 1865 probably exceeded those of any other mercantile house in the world. Southern interests embarrassed the firm at the Civil War's start and in the panic of 1873, yet he paid every dollar of his liabilities. That promptness raised his reputation for ability and integrity, and he died at Fordham on 14 November 1885.
britannica-1911-cobham:
Cobham is a village in the Medway division of Kent, England, four miles west of Rochester, and its church is famous for a collection of ancient brasses. Thirteen brasses of the years 1320 to 1529 commemorate members of the Brooke and Cobham families there. Fine oak stalls and some tilting armour of the 14th century stand in the chancel. Cobham College, holding twenty almshouses, replaced a college for priests founded by Sir John de Cobham.

The present mansion of Cobham Hall is mainly Elizabethan, and its picture gallery holds a fine collection by Italian, Dutch and English masters. The Cobham family was established here before the reign of King John, and Henry de Cobham was created Baron Cobham in 1313. After Oldcastle's execution in 1417 the barony lay dormant until revived in 1445. Henry Brooke, Lord Cobham, was arraigned in 1603 for the Raleigh conspiracy and died in prison in 1618.
britannica-1911-cockerill-william:
Anglo French inventor William Cockerill, born in England in seventeen fifty nine, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He went to Belgium as a plain mechanic. In seventeen ninety nine he built the first wool carding and spinning machines on the mainland of Europe at Verviers.

In eighteen oh seven he set up a large machine works at Liege. Orders came in from all over Europe, and he grew rich. Napoleon gave him French citizenship rights in eighteen ten. Two years later he handed the firm to his youngest son John. John built vast works at Seraing, with an iron foundry and blast furnace. Belgian rail building from eighteen thirty four gave those works a great boost.
britannica-1911-cofferdam:
A cofferdam is a work of engineering used to lay foundations under water. The engineer rings the site with a bank or dam. Water is then shut out of the space inside. Pumps clear what stays, and work can start on dry ground. Depth and current decide how strong the dam must be.

Where water is shallow and the flow slight, plain clay dams can serve. Most cases call for a stouter build. Two rows of piles form the walls. Clay puddle fills the gap between them. The whole mass must bear the push of the water outside once the inside is pumped dry. The entry keeps to that core plan. It points to foundations for fuller treatment of the work that follows.
britannica-1911-coldstream:
Coldstream, a police burgh of Berwickshire in Scotland, gets a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It stands on the north bank of the Tweed, at Smeaton's fine five arch bridge of 1763 to 1766. Its count in 1901 was 1,482 people. Town hall, library, a mechanics' institute, and a cottage hospital serve it, and some brewing goes on.

As the first ford of weight above Berwick, the town stood in the path of armies. Edward the First crossed here in 1296, and Montrose in 1640. A priory founded about 1165 was wrecked in 1545. In 1659 General Monk raised here the famed Foot Guards that bear its name. Like Gretna Green, the town drew runaway couples to wed at the toll house, and that Marriage House still stands.
britannica-1911-colenso-john-william:
John William Colenso, an English bishop of Natal who lived from 1814 to 1883, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Saint Austell in Cornwall, he came from a family in straitened means. Kin gave him the means for a university education. In 1836 he placed high in mathematics at Cambridge and became a fellow the next year.

He went to Harrow as a teacher of mathematics, but the move went badly. The school was at a low ebb, he had few pupils, and a fire cost him most of his property. Back at Cambridge, he paid off heavy debts by hard tutoring. His manuals of algebra and arithmetic were taken up all over England. In 1853 he was made bishop of Natal, where he learned Zulu and made a grammar, a dictionary, and translations.
britannica-1911-combe-william:
William Combe is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English writer. He lived from 1741 to 1823. He was the creator of the character Doctor Syntax. He was born at Bristol in the year 1741. The facts of his birth and parentage are doubtful. His father may have been a rich Bristol merchant. He may have been a London alderman named Alexander. Combe was educated at Eton in his youth.

An inheritance of some two thousand pounds came to him. That small fortune soon vanished in splendid extravagance. The spending gained him the nickname of Count Combe. His career then ran through many odd turns. He served as soldier, cook, and waiter at times. About 1771 he settled in London for good. There he studied law and wrote for booksellers. Debts later brought him into the King's Bench prison.
britannica-1911-congreve-sir-william:
Sir William Congreve (1772–1828) was a British artillerist and inventor born on 20 May 1772. His father ran the Royal Laboratory at Woolwich as comptroller. The son was schooled in Kent and at Trinity College, Cambridge. He took degrees there in 1793 and 1795. He then entered the Middle Temple and lived in Garden Court until 1808.

Law held him first, then a political newspaper. In the end the war rocket took all his zeal. That weapon made his name for good. His father's post gave him rare scope to test guns and gear. In 1805 he showed the new weapon to the prince regent and Pitt. That year he joined a naval attack on the French flotilla at Boulogne. Weather blocked the rockets then. In a fresh attack in 1806 they were fired in earnest.
britannica-1911-congreve-william:
William Congreve (1670–1729) was an English dramatist, called the greatest English master of pure comedy. He was baptized at Bardsey near Leeds on 10 February 1670. His stone gives his birth year as 1672. His father was a soldier soon sent to command the garrison at Youghal. Ireland thus claims the credit for his schooling.

He learned at Kilkenny, then at Dublin, where Swift was his friend and fellow student. In London he read law at the Middle Temple. His first work was a novel under a boyish pen name. Johnson is said to have quipped that he would rather praise it than read it. In 1693 his true career began with The Old Bachelor. That first comedy met instant success. The entry traces the plays that made his fame, and weighs one venture into tragedy as well.
britannica-1911-conjeeveram:
Conjeeveram, also called Kanchipuram, is a town in the Madras region of India. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica ranks it among the seven sacred cities held dear by Hindus. Temples and shrines crowd the town. Silk and cotton saris woven there were prized for their fine quality.

Two old temple groups draw most of the note. One honors Vishnu and one honors Siva, and both date from Pallava times. A great hall said to hold a thousand columns in fact holds 540 carved posts. A long dispute over a temple mark led to court cases and still caused unrest when the entry was written.
britannica-1911-cookworthy-william:
William Cookworthy (1705–1780) was an English potter famed for finding china-clay and china-stone in Cornwall. He was the first maker of a porcelain like the Chinese ware from English materials. He was born at Kingsbridge in Devon, of Quaker parents in humble means. At fourteen he was set to a London apothecary named Bevans. He later traded at Plymouth with his old master.

Porcelain drew much English interest in his day. Bow, Chelsea, Worcester and Derby made a glassy ware by craft. Cookworthy took a plainer path, guided by the reports of Père d'Entrecolles. He spent years in search of English stuff like that used in China. From 1745 he ranged most of Cornwall and Devon on that hunt. He found the minerals at last in the parish of Saint Stephen. The entry rates his Plymouth ware low as art, yet grants its sound craft.
britannica-1911-cornwallis-sir-william:
Sir William Cornwallis, a British admiral who lived from 1744 to 1819, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the brother of the first Marquess Cornwallis, governor general of India. Born in February 1744, he entered the navy in 1755. Promotion came fast, and he reached post rank in 1766.

Until 1779 Cornwallis did the plain work of the navy on convoy duty. That year his ship Lion was mauled in battle off Grenada and had to reach Jamaica alone. He fought French forces twice more near America in 1780. Later he served at the relief of Gibraltar and at the battle of Dominica in 1782. From 1788 to 1794 he served in the East Indies and helped take Pondicherry. His fame rests on a retreat in June 1795. Chased by a far larger French fleet near Brest, he brought his small force off with skill.
britannica-1911-corson-hiram:
Hiram Corson is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an American scholar born in Philadelphia in eighteen twenty eight. He first worked in the great state library at the capital of his land. He then taught English letters at schools and colleges for years.

The entry lists his long chair at a new university in New York state. A chair of English letters was formed there for him in time. He cut school sets of Chaucer tales and wrote guides to old English. Handbooks on verse, speech craft, and famed poets bear his name. His notes on the Bard draw praise as keen and sound work.
britannica-1911-coventry-sir-william:
Sir William Coventry (about 1628–1686) was an English statesman, son of Thomas, Lord Coventry, the lord keeper. He entered Queen's College, Oxford, at age fourteen to matriculate. The outbreak of the Civil War forced him to quit his studies. A good tutor had made him a scholar all the same, one witness holds. Travel gave him a fine command of French.

While the war ran on, he joined the army before its end and led a company of foot. He then went to France and stayed there for years. He came home when hope of foreign help and a fresh army had died. Through the Commonwealth years he kept clear of royalist plots. When a restoration looked near in 1660, he hastened to Breda. James, duke of York, took him as secretary in that year. He headed the royal procession when Charles entered London in triumph.
britannica-1911-cowley-abraham:
Abraham Cowley (1618–1667) was an English poet born in the city of London late in 1618. His father was a wealthy stationer who died just before his birth. His mother gave her days to works of devotion. A copy of The Faery Queen lay in her parlour by chance. That book became the boy's favourite reading. He had read it through twice before he went to school.

In 1628, in his tenth year, he wrote his first long poem. The Tragicall History of Piramus and Thisbe is an epic romance in a six-line stanza of his own making. It shows no great fault of youth, it holds, and its build is of a high order. Two years later came Constantia and Philetus, a still larger aim. At Westminster school his gifts showed in full. At thirteen he wrote an elegy on a school patron's death.
britannica-1911-cox-sir-george-william:
Sir George William Cox (1827–1902) was an English divine and scholar born at Benares in India on 10 January 1827. He was schooled at Rugby and at Trinity College, Oxford. In 1850 he was ordained. In 1860 he took a mastership at Cheltenham College, but held it for one year only. Print had claimed him before that post.

He had written for the Edinburgh Review by then. Poems, Legendary and Historical came in 1850, with E. A. Freeman as his partner. A Life of Saint Boniface followed in 1853. From 1861 he gave himself to literary work in full. History and comparative mythology formed his chief fields. His works spoke to a broad public by design. His History of Greece has been superseded and holds little value now, the entry grants. Max Müller lit his zeal for myth. He backed the solar theory of myth to an extreme. He gained the baronetcy in 1877.
britannica-1911-croft-william:
William Croft (1678–1727) was an English composer born at Nether Ettington in Warwickshire. He trained in the Chapel Royal under Dr Blow and became organist of St Anne's, Soho, while still young. In 1707 he was made joint organist of the Chapel Royal with Blow. On Blow's death in 1708 he took the post alone, with the mastership of the children and the organist's place at Westminster Abbey. Oxford gave him a doctorate in music in 1713.

In 1724 Croft published his choral music as Musica Sacra, in two folio volumes. It held anthems for two to eight voices plus the Burial Service used at Westminster Abbey. The work was the first of its kind printed in score on pewter plates. He also published airs for violins, sonatas and solos for flute, and early theatre music. He died at Bath on 14 August 1727 and lies in Westminster Abbey under a monument.
britannica-1911-crookes-sir-william:
Sir William Crookes (born 1832) was an English chemist and physicist born in London on 17 June 1832. He studied chemistry at the Royal College of Chemistry under Hofmann and became his assistant in 1851. Posts at the Radcliffe observatory and at Chester followed. In 1861 a bright green line in a spectrum led him to isolate a new element, thallium. He spent eight years studying that metal and its properties.

While weighing thallium in a vacuum, Crookes found the balance acted strangely, and he explained the effect as repulsion from radiation. From that principle he built the radiometer. His work on electric discharge in highly exhausted tubes, the Crookes tubes, led to his theory of radiant matter, a fourth state that pointed toward the electronic theory. From 1883 he studied the rare earths and claimed to split the yttrium molecule. Knighted in 1897, he held the Royal, Davy, and Copley medals of the Royal Society.
britannica-1911-crosskey-henry-william:
Henry William Crosskey (1826–1893) was an English geologist and Unitarian minister born at Lewes in Sussex on 7 December 1826. Trained for the ministry at Manchester New College, he held pastorates at Derby, Glasgow, and Birmingham. At Birmingham he served the Church of the Messiah until his death. Ramsay's Geology of the Isle of Arran first drew him to geology while he lived in Glasgow. From 1855 he gave his leisure to that science.

Crosskey became an authority on glacial geology, writing much with David Robertson on the post-tertiary fossil beds of Scotland. His reports on erratic blocks across England, Wales, and Ireland ran from 1873 to 1892 for the British Association. With Robertson and Brady he wrote a monograph on the post-tertiary Entomostraca of Scotland in 1874. He also edited Carvill Lewis's papers on glacial geology after that writer's death. He died at Edgbaston on 1 October 1893.
britannica-1911-crotch-william:
William Crotch (1775–1847) was an English musician born in Norwich on 5 July 1775, the son of a master carpenter. At little more than two he played tunes on an organ his father had built. At four he gave daily organ recitals in rooms in Piccadilly. In 1789, aged fourteen, his oratorio The Captivity of Judah was performed at Cambridge. He became organist of Christ Church, Oxford, in 1790.

At twenty-two Crotch was professor of music at Oxford, and he took his doctorate there in 1799. He lectured at Oxford and at the Royal Institution, and in 1822 he became principal of the London Royal Academy of Music. His best work is the oratorio Palestine of 1812. He also published specimens of musical styles, lectures, and a manual of composition. The entry judges that his infant promise went unfulfilled, though he stayed a sound and busy artist. He died at Taunton on 29 December 1847.
britannica-1911-crozier-william:
William Crozier (born 1855) was an American artillerist and inventor from Ohio. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes his father served as Kansas chief justice and senator. West Point gave him his degree in 1876 as an artillery officer. Frontier war against Sioux and Bannock filled his first three years.

He taught mathematics at West Point, then ran Watertown Arsenal in turn. A tour to study European guns in 1888 set his life course. With Buffington he devised the disappearing gun carriage in 1896 for coasts. Wire wound guns and ordnance gear bear his stamp as well. Hague delegate and ordnance chief by 1901 round out the record.
britannica-1911-cubitt-sir-william:
Sir William Cubitt (1785–1861) was an English engineer born at Dilham in Norfolk, where his father was a miller. He served four years as a joiner and cabinetmaker, then joined an agricultural-machine maker. In 1807 he patented self-regulating sails for windmills. At the Ransome works in Ipswich he rose to chief engineer and partner. About 1818 he introduced the treadmill, his device for employing criminals.

From 1826 Cubitt practised in London on a large scale. His works include the Oxford canal, the improvement of the Severn, docks at Cardiff and Middlesborough, and the South-Eastern railway. Berlin's water-works were built under his eye, and foreign governments consulted him on harbours and railways. In 1851, while president of the Institution of Civil Engineers, he was knighted for service to the Hyde Park exhibition buildings. He died at Clapham on 13 October 1861, and the entry adds his son Joseph, a railway engineer.
britannica-1911-cullen-william:
William Cullen (1710–1790) was a Scottish physician and medical teacher born at Hamilton in Lanarkshire on 15 April 1710. Apprenticed to a Glasgow surgeon, he served as surgeon on a merchant ship to the West Indies. He studied at Edinburgh from 1734 and helped found the Royal Medical Society. Practice at Hamilton won him a high name, and William Hunter was his resident pupil there. In 1744 he removed to Glasgow and began to lecture.

Cullen lectured on medicine, botany, materia medica, and chemistry, and his classes grew fast. Joseph Black was among the pupils his zeal for research fired. In 1756 he became professor of chemistry at Edinburgh, a chair he held for ten years. The tail of the entry sets out his classing of diseases in four orders. Fevers, nervous diseases, wasting diseases of bad habit, and local diseases make up that scheme. His son Robert became a Scottish judge as Lord Cullen in 1796.
britannica-1911-dale-robert-william:
Robert William Dale, an English Nonconformist divine who lived from 1829 to 1895, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London on 1 December 1829, he was educated at Spring Hill College in Birmingham. In 1853 he was invited to Carr Lane Chapel in Birmingham as co pastor.

On the death of his senior colleague in 1859 Dale became sole pastor of Carr Lane for the rest of his life. In the London University examination of 1853 he stood first in philosophy and won the gold medal. Glasgow gave him a doctorate in law during the rectorship of John Bright. Yale gave him a doctorate in divinity, which he never used by his own choice. Dale took a keen interest in Liberal politics and in the municipal affairs of Birmingham.
britannica-1911-dampier-william:
William Dampier (1652–1715) was an English buccaneer, navigator, and hydrographer born at East Coker in Somersetshire. Orphaned early, he shipped from Weymouth to Newfoundland, then to the East Indies. He fought in the Dutch War of 1673, worked briefly on a Jamaica estate, and learned the island's ports in the coasting trade. Voyages to Campeachy and time with the logwood-cutters mixed into buccaneering. In 1679 he joined the buccaneers who crossed Darien to the Pacific.

Dampier raided the Peruvian coast, sailed with Cook and then Davis and Swan, and crossed the Pacific in 1686 toward the East Indies. The long entry follows his later voyages, including the voyage to New Holland in 1699. His books, led by A New Voyage Round the World of 1697, made his name at home. The entry praises his style as easy, clear, and manly. His knowledge of natural history, though unscientific, is judged surprisingly exact and trustworthy.
britannica-1911-dar-es-salaam:
Dar-es-Salaam, the harbour of peace, is a seaport of East Africa and the capital of German East Africa. Its people numbered about 24,000 in 1909, some 500 of them Europeans, and a narrow opening in the palm-covered shore leads into its perfectly sheltered harbour. A floating dock was finished in 1902, and wide regular streets, government offices, the governor's house, a hospital and botanical gardens give the town a European look.

Sultan Said Majid of Zanzibar began a palace there in 1862 but died in 1871 with the scheme dropped. German occupation followed in 1887, the imperial government took over in 1889, and the town became the colony's capital in 1891. Ivory, rubber and copal lead its exports, though trade grew slowly.
britannica-1911-eliot-charles-william:
Charles William Eliot, the Harvard chief, is set out in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Boston in 1834, he was a mayor's son of that city. He finished Harvard in 1853 and taught chemistry there for years. Two years in Europe taught him how schools ran abroad in depth. A new tech school in Boston then took him as its teacher.

In 1869 Eliot was picked to lead Harvard at a young age. A layman and a man of science held that post for once. Graduate schools grew strong at Harvard under his firm hand. His plan of free choice in studies spread far and wide. Entrance bars rose, and high schools rose to meet them in turn.
britannica-1911-ellery-william:
Ellery, William (1727–1820), was an American politician and a signer of the Declaration of Independence, born in Newport, Rhode Island, on 22 December 1727. He graduated from Harvard in 1747, went into trade, then studied law and was admitted to the bar in 1770. He sat on the Rhode Island committee of safety in 1775 and 1776. Congress received him as a delegate in 1776, just after his first election.

Ellery served in Congress from 1776 to 1781 and again from 1783 to 1785. He was placed on the marine committee and, when a board of admiralty was set up in 1779, he joined that board too. In April 1786 he became commissioner of the continental loan office for Rhode Island. From 1790 until his death he was collector of the customs for the district of Newport. He died at Newport on 15 February 1820, closing a long public life that ran from colonial trade to the customs service of the new republic.
britannica-1911-elliston-robert-william:
Elliston, Robert William (1774–1831), was an English actor born in London on 7 April 1774, the son of a watchmaker. Educated at St Paul's school, he ran away from home and first appeared on stage as Tressel in Richard III at Bath in 1791. He was later seen there as Romeo and in other leading parts, comic and tragic. From 1796 he repeated his successes in London.

Elliston acted at Drury Lane from 1804 to 1809 and again from 1812, and from 1819 he was lessee of the house, presenting Kean, Mme Vestris, and Macready. Ill health and misfortune ended in his bankruptcy in 1826, when he made his last Drury Lane appearance as Falstaff. As lessee of the Surrey theatre he acted almost until his death. Leigh Hunt compared him favourably with Garrick, Byron thought him inimitable in high comedy, and Macready praised his range. He also wrote plays, among them The Venetian Outlaw of 1805.
britannica-1911-elphinstone-william:
Elphinstone, William (1431–1514), was a Scottish statesman and churchman, founder of the university of Aberdeen, born in Glasgow and educated at its university. After brief practice as a lawyer in the church courts he was ordained priest. He became rector of St Michael's, Trongate, Glasgow, in 1465.

Elphinstone became bishop of Ross in 1481 and bishop of Aberdeen in 1483. James III sent him on embassies to Louis XI of France and Edward IV of England. He was made lord high chancellor early in 1488, then keeper of the privy seal in 1492 under James IV. His closing years went chiefly to founding the university of Aberdeen. The papal bull came in 1494 and the royal charter in 1498, and King's College was completed in 1506. The entry also credits him with a part in bringing printing into Scotland. He died at Edinburgh on 25 October 1514.
britannica-1911-epigram:
Epigram, strictly speaking, is anything that is inscribed. The long entry opens by warning that no definition can cover the host of little poems honoured with the title. Yet none can stay tight enough to shut out all others. It finds the name given in four ways. First, it covers any true inscription on a monument, statue, or building. Second, it covers verses never meant for stone but cast in inscription form for art's sake.

Third, the name covers verses that voice a striking or fine thought with inscription-like brevity. Fourth, by a narrowing the entry calls unwarranted, it covers a little poem ending in a “point,” above all a satirical one. Lessing's two-part doctrine, a first part that wakes attention like a monument and a second that answers it in an unexpected way, is treated with more respect.
britannica-1911-etty-william:
William Etty (1787–1849) was a British painter born at York on 10 March 1787. His father ended as a York baker of spice-bread. At eleven and a half Etty left home for a seven-year printing apprenticeship at the Hull Packet. He practised drawing in secret, then by his master's leave. A copy of Cupid and Psyche shown to Opie won him entry to the Academy schools in 1807.

His uncle paid 100 guineas for private tuition under Sir Thomas Lawrence. Rejection followed rejection until Telemachus Rescuing Antiope hung at the Academy in 1811, badly placed and little noticed. A three-month Italian trip in 1816 cut short, he still rose slowly. In the summer of 1849 he showed a hall full of his works in London. He died on 13 November that year and had a public funeral at York. The entry praises his colour and feeling above his drawing.
britannica-1911-ewart-william:
William Ewart, an English politician who lived from 1798 to 1869, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Liverpool, he was schooled at Eton and Christ Church, Oxford, and won the Newdigate prize for verse. He was called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1827. The next year he entered parliament for Bletchingley, and later sat for Liverpool, Wigan, and Dumfries Burghs.

Ewart, an advanced liberal, carried a long list of useful bills. In 1834 he ended hanging in chains, and in 1837 he won an act that ended death as the price for cattle stealing. In 1850 he carried the bill for free libraries paid from the rates. In 1864 he helped make the metric system legal. He fought to end capital punishment and backed yearly reports on schooling and open exams for state posts.
britannica-1911-faber-frederick-william:
Frederick William Faber, who lived from 1814 to 1863, was a British hymn writer. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Calverley in Yorkshire. His grandfather had been vicar of that place. School at Harrow and college at Oxford followed. In 1836 he won the Newdigate prize for a poem. Keble praised that poem in special terms. At Oxford he fell under the sway of John Henry Newman.

A post as a travelling tutor took him abroad in 1841. A book from that trip won Wordsworth's favour. He took a rectory, then went abroad again to study Rome's methods. After a long inner struggle he joined the Roman church in 1845. He founded a brotherhood at Birmingham that merged with Newman's oratory. From 1849 he led the London oratory at Brompton.
britannica-1911-fairbairn-sir-william:
Sir William Fairbairn is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a Scottish engineer. He lived from 1789 to 1874. He was born at Kelso in Roxburghshire. His father was a farm bailiff in that town. In 1803 he got work as a mason's labourer. The work was on a bridge Rennie was building at Kelso. Within days an accident put him out of action.

Later that year his father took a steward's post at a colliery farm. The place was Percy Main Colliery near North Shields. The son got work there as a carter. In March 1804 he was bound apprentice to a millwright. At Percy Main he found time for private study. He used it to fill the gaps in his schooling. There he also made the acquaintance of George Stephenson. Stephenson then had charge of an engine at a near colliery.
britannica-1911-falconer-william:
William Falconer, a British poet and sailor who lived from 1732 to 1769, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Edinburgh, the son of a wig maker who sank into deep want. The boy got thin schooling and was sent to sea young. At eighteen he was second mate of a ship in the Levant trade.

That ship was wrecked in a dread storm off Cape Colonna, and only three men lived. Falconer was one of the three, and the wreck gave him his famed poem, The Shipwreck. It came out in 1762 and won him a patron in the duke of York. He then served in the royal navy as a midshipman and purser. In 1769 his great dictionary of the sea was printed.
britannica-1911-farnham:
Farnham is a Surrey market town on the river Wey, 37 and a half miles south-west by west of London. Its urban district held 6,124 people in 1901. The church of St Andrew is a roomy building of transitional Norman and Early English work. Beside the town stand the remains of Waverley Abbey, the earliest Cistercian house in England, founded in 1128 by Bishop William Gifford. Its annals are thought to have given Scott the name Waverley.

Farnham Castle, seat of the bishops of Winchester, was first built by Henry de Blois. Henry III razed it; Waller took the rebuilt castle in 1642, and Bishop Morley restored it after dismantling. William Cobbett was born in the parish in 1766 and lies in St Andrew's churchyard. At Moor Park Sir William Temple kept Swift as secretary. The bishop granted the first charter in 1247. Hop-growing nearby began in 1597, and fine hops still mark the district.
britannica-1911-faversham:
Faversham is a market town and river-port in Kent, England, a member of the Cinque Port of Dover, on a creek of the Swale nine miles west-north-west of Canterbury. Its 1901 population was 11,290. The church of St Mary of Charity, restored by Sir G. G. Scott in 1874, is Early English, with fresco remains, fine brasses and a tomb said to be King Stephen's. He was buried at the abbey he founded here in 1147.

Faversham Creek takes vessels of 200 tons, and trade in coal, timber and farm produce is considerable. Its oyster fisheries, run by an ancient gild of dredgermen, are important, alongside brewing, brickmaking, cement and powder mills nearby. The entry traces the town from a Romano-British village and royal demesne in 1086, noting its grammar school of 1527 and its government by mayor, aldermen and councillors over 686 acres.
britannica-1911-ferguson-adam:
Adam Ferguson, a Scottish thinker and historian who lived from 1723 to 1816, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Logierait in Perthshire and schooled at Perth and at Saint Andrews. In 1745 his knowledge of Gaelic won him a post as deputy chaplain to the Black Watch. At Fontenoy that year he fought in the ranks all day.

He stayed with the regiment until 1754, then left the clergy for a life of letters. In 1757 he followed David Hume as librarian to the faculty of advocates. In 1759 he became professor of natural philosophy at Edinburgh. Five years later he moved to the chair of mental and moral philosophy. His Essay on the History of Civil Society, in 1767, was well received across Europe. He wrote it against Hume's advice, and it was translated into several tongues.
britannica-1911-fergusson-sir-william:
Sir William Fergusson, a British surgeon who lived from 1808 to 1877, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Prestonpans in East Lothian on 20 March 1808, he was the son of James Fergusson of Lochmaben. He was schooled at Lochmaben and at the high school of Edinburgh. He entered Edinburgh university to study law, then soon gave that up for medicine.

Fergusson became a pupil of the anatomist Robert Knox and his demonstrator at age twenty. In 1836 he followed Robert Liston as surgeon to the Edinburgh Royal Infirmary. In 1840 he came to London as professor of surgery at Kings College and surgeon to its hospital. There he won a commanding place among the surgeons of the capital. He revived the operation for cleft palate, long in disrepute, and invented a mouth gag for it.
britannica-1911-fitz-osbern-william:
William Fitz-Osbern, the chief Norman helper of the Conquest, gets a brief life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a close friend of William the Conqueror. He did more than most to set up the crossing to England. His reward was the earldom of Hereford on the Welsh border. His set task there was to push the Norman reach into Wales.

In 1067 Fitz-Osbern stood as William's deputy in mid England. He guarded that land from the Welsh and from the Danes. He served again as deputy in the risings of 1069. Sent to help rule Normandy in 1070, he took a new path. A rich widow of Flanders won him with an offer of marriage. He died in 1071, fighting for her cause at Cassel.
britannica-1911-fleetwood-william:
William Fleetwood (1656-1723), English divine, came from an old Lancashire family and was born in the Tower of London on New Year's Day 1656. He was educated at Eton and at King's College, Cambridge. About the time of the Revolution he took orders. He soon became rector of St Austin's, London, and lecturer at St Dunstan's in the West. He was made a canon of Windsor in 1702, bishop of St Asaph in 1708, and was moved to Ely in 1714.

Fleetwood was counted the best preacher of his time, accurate in learning and strong in delivery, and his character stood high. As a bishop he far excelled most men of his day. A zealous Hanoverian and a Whig, he still kept Queen Anne's favour. His stand against non-resistance clashed with the Tory ministry of 1712 and with Swift. His writings include an Essay on Miracles and a work on English coinage. He died in 1723.
britannica-1911-fonblanque-albany-willia:
Albany William Fonblanque (1793-1872), English journalist, came of a noble French Huguenot family, the Greniers of Languedoc. He was born in London in 1793. His grandfather, a banker, took the name Fonblanque on becoming English. His father, John Samuel Martin Fonblanque, was a noted equity lawyer, author of a standard Treatise on Equity, and a member of parliament. Albany was sent to Woolwich at fourteen to prepare for the Royal Engineers, but his health failed.

After two lost years Fonblanque studied for the bar, then began writing for newspapers at nineteen, in 1812. He won notice at once for bold, liberal opinions and a style far above the daily press of the day. From 1820 to 1830 he worked for The Times, the Morning Chronicle, the Examiner and other papers. The entry's opening pages appear at the end of the hosted Fonblanque file and continue in the next file, following his rise in London journalism.
britannica-1911-fordham:
Fordham was formerly a village of Westchester county, New York, and is now part of New York City. It lies on the mainland along the east bank of the Harlem river, east of the northern end of Manhattan Island. It is the seat of Fordham University, a Roman Catholic institution founded in 1841 as St John's College. Since 1846 the Society of Jesus has run it. In 1907 it was rechartered as Fordham University, with college, medical school and a law school on Broadway.

In 1907-1908 the university had 96 instructors and 236 students, besides 364 boys in its high school. Fordham still holds the house where Edgar Allan Poe lived from 1844 to 1849 and wrote Annabel Lee and Ulalume. The entry then traces the hamlet's past: John Archer settled sixteen families there in 1669 by a ford of Spuyten Duyvil Creek, and the tract became the manor of Fordham in 1671. It joined New York City in 1874.
britannica-1911-fowler-william:
William Fowler (about 1560-1614), Scottish poet, was born about the year 1560. He attended St Leonard's College, St Andrews, between 1574 and 1578. In 1581 he was in Paris studying civil law. That year he issued a pamphlet against John Hamilton and other Catholics, who had, he said, driven him from his country. About 1590 he became private secretary and Master of Requests to Anne of Denmark, wife of James VI, and he kept those offices when the queen went to England.

In 1609 Fowler's services were rewarded with a grant of 2,000 acres in Ulster. His sister Susannah married Sir John Drummond and was mother of the poet William Drummond of Hawthornden. On the title-page of his Triumphs of Petrarke, Fowler styles himself P. of Hawick, often taken to mean parson of Hawick. The notice stands in a shared Fowler file, after the two engineering Fowlers.
britannica-1911-framingham:
Framingham is a township of Middlesex county, Massachusetts, with an area of 27 square miles of hilly surface dotted with lakes and ponds. Its population grew from 9,239 in 1890 to 12,948 in 1910, with 2,391 foreign-born residents in 1900. The Boston and Albany and the New York, New Haven and Hartford railways serve it. Within the township lie three villages: Framingham Center, Saxonville and South Framingham, the last by far the most important of the three for trade and people.

Framingham Academy was founded in 1792 and joined the public school system in 1851. A state normal school stands here, the first in the United States, founded at Lexington in 1839 and moved to Framingham in 1853. Near South Framingham stands the state reformatory prison for women. South Framingham makes paper tags, shoes and boilers in large works. The entry gives a New England mill township in the full Edwardian manner, schools, prisons and factories together.
britannica-1911-framlingham:
Framlingham is a market town in the Eye division of Suffolk, 91 miles north-east of London by a branch of the Great Eastern railway. Its population in 1901 was 2,526. The church of St Michael is a fine building of black flint in the Perpendicular and Decorated styles, crowned by a tower 96 feet high. Inside are notable monuments, above all those of Thomas Howard, third duke of Norfolk, and of Henry Howard, the earl of Surrey, whom Henry VIII beheaded, the poet of the family.

The castle is a picturesque ruin: outer walls 44 feet high and eight feet thick, thirteen towers about 58 feet high, a gateway and outworks. Half a mile away stands the Albert Memorial Middle Class College, opened in 1865 for 300 boys, with a bronze statue of the Prince Consort on its terrace. The entry then traces the town from early Saxon times, when its name was spelled Frendlingham or Framalingaham.
britannica-1911-frere-john-hookham:
John Hookham Frere (1769-1846), English diplomatist and author, was born in London on 21 May 1769. At Eton he formed the friendship with Canning that shaped his life, and at Cambridge he took his degree in 1792. He entered the foreign office under Grenville and sat in parliament for West Looe from 1796 to 1802.

With Canning he wrote for the Anti-Jacobin, producing parodies such as The Loves of the Triangles and The Needy Knife-Grinder. He served as envoy at Lisbon in 1800 and Madrid in 1802, and in 1808 went back to Spain to the Central Junta. His urgent advice to Sir John Moore before the retreat to Corunna drew public blame and ended his career. Settled in Malta from 1820, he turned to letters. His verse renderings of Aristophanes are still prized, and Byron took from his mock-heroic Whistlecraft poem the measure later perfected in Don Juan.
britannica-1911-fulke-william:
Fulke, William (1538–1589), an English Puritan divine, was educated at St John's College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow in 1564. He took a leading part in the vestiarian controversy, persuading the college to discard the surplice, and was expelled from St John's for a time in consequence. In 1567 he became Hebrew lecturer and preacher there. Leicester made him his chaplain, and in 1578 he was elected master of Pembroke Hall.

In 1581 Fulke was one of the disputants with the Jesuit Edmund Campion. His Defense of the sincere and true Translations of 1583 answered Roman Catholic attacks on the English Bible. His many polemical writings also confuted Thomas Stapleton, Cardinal Allen and other Roman Catholic controversialists.
britannica-1911-fuller-william:
Fuller, William (1670–1717), an English impostor, was born at Milton in Kent on the 20th of September 1670. He served Mary of Modena and the Jacobite cause while at the same time courting the favour of William III. In 1692 the House of Commons declared him an impostor, a cheat and a false accuser, and he stood in the pillory. He later revived the story that Mary of Modena was not the true mother of the prince of Wales.

Fuller's Life of himself appeared in 1701. He was again pilloried, whipped and fined, and he died about 1717, probably in prison.
britannica-1911-gascoigne-sir-william:
Sir William Gascoigne (about 1350-1419) was chief justice of England under Henry IV. The 1911 Britannica entry presents him as a great lawyer who held that the head of the state is subject to law. He came of an old Yorkshire family and practised as an advocate under Edward III and Richard II.

In 1405 Henry IV pressed him to sentence Archbishop Scrope and the earl marshal for revolt. Gascoigne refused, holding that they must be tried by their peers. Both were executed without him. The entry also treats the famous tale of him sending the prince of Wales to prison as unauthentic, though in character. He left office soon after Henry V came to the throne and died in 1419, buried at Harewood in Yorkshire.
britannica-1911-gaul-gilbert-william:
Gilbert William Gaul (1855- ) was an American artist, born in Jersey City, New Jersey, on 31 March 1855. The 1911 Britannica entry names his teachers as J. G. Brown and L. E. Wilmarth. He became a painter of military pictures, drawing his scenes from incidents of the American Civil War.

Honours came early: associate of the National Academy of Design in 1880, and full academician in 1882. In that same year he joined the Society of American Artists. The entry closes with a list of his chief works. They include Charging the Battery, News from Home, Cold Comfort on the Outpost, Silenced, On the Look-out, and Guerillas returning from a Raid. It is a short career notice, with the list of pictures carrying most of the weight.
britannica-1911-ged-william:
William Ged (1690-1749) was the inventor of stereotyping, born at Edinburgh in 1690. The 1911 Britannica entry says he patented his process in 1725, building on Van der Mey's idea of soldering loose types together. He succeeded in casting a whole page of type in similar metal.

Edinburgh printers would not take the process up, so Ged went into partnership with a London stationer and a typefounder. The partnership went badly, and the entry blames trade jealousy and the compositors' dislike of the new method. Ged died in poverty on 19 October 1749. Two Cambridge prayer-books and an edition of Sallust were printed from his plates. His sons later carried the patent on, and Andrew Wilson perfected it.
britannica-1911-gib-adam:
Adam Gib, a Scots churchman who lived from 1714 to 1788, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in the parish of Muckhart in Perthshire, he studied at Edinburgh and Perth. He was licensed as a preacher in 1740 and ordained in 1741. His charge was the large Secession congregation of Bristo Street in Edinburgh.

In 1745 Gib was near the sole minister in Edinburgh who kept preaching against revolt while rebel troops held the town. A split in his church came in 1747 over the Burgess Oath and how fast to act on a ruling against it. Gib led the side that broke away, and the new Antiburgher Synod was formed in his own house. He led that section of the Secession Church from then on, and his sway over its acts was great, the text says.
britannica-1911-gilbart-james-william:
James William Gilbart, who lived from 1794 to 1863, was an English banking writer. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his rise in joint stock banking. He was born in London in March 1794. He clerked in a London bank from 1813 to 1825.

Branch posts in Ireland trained Gilbart for a bigger stage. In 1834 he became manager of the London and Westminster Bank. He did much to grow the joint stock bank system. His witness work before Parliament helped that cause more than once. A clause he won in 1844 let such banks sue by an officer. It also let them take bills at short dates. His banking books ran through many editions at home. Named lectures at Kings College still honor his memory.
britannica-1911-gilbert-william:
William Gilbert (1544-1603) was the leading English man of science of Elizabeth's reign, and, the 1911 Britannica entry says, the father of electric and magnetic science. He was born at Colchester on 24 May 1544, of an old Suffolk family. At St John's College, Cambridge, he took his degrees and his medical doctorate in 1569.

After three years in Italy and Europe he settled in London in 1573 and practised medicine with great success. College of Physicians offices followed: censor, treasurer, and president in 1599. In 1601 he became physician to Queen Elizabeth. The entry's opening then sets up the work behind his fame in magnetic and electric study, for which he is named the father of both sciences. His move to court late in life closes the part of the account read here.
britannica-1911-goffe-william:
William Goffe was an English soldier and lawmaker who backed Parliament in the civil war. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his story. He was the son of a Puritan rector in Essex. He first trained with a London salt seller, then joined the army in 1645.

Goffe helped bring King Charles to trial and signed his death warrant. He fought at Dunbar and Worcester and rose to major general. He sat in Parliament, served on state councils, and backed Oliver Cromwell to the end. When the king came back in 1660, Goffe fled to Massachusetts. He lived in exile apart from his family and died there, it is thought, near 1679.
britannica-1911-gram:
Gram, the chick-pea of warm lands, is set out in a plant entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The plant goes by many names, from Bengal gram to garbanzo. Its Latin name notes how the seed looks like a ram's head. It belongs to the pea family and feeds crowds as a pulse. Farms grow it in south Europe, Egypt, and Asia to India.

The herb lives one year, with bent stems and split leaves. Its blooms are blue-purple and borne one to a stalk. The pod swells to hold two round seeds. Greeks grew it in Homer's time under an old name. Romans called it cicer, the root of names still used in the south.
britannica-1911-grantham:
Grantham is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a borough town in Lincolnshire in England, on a small river. Rail lines meet there and a canal links it to a larger river town. A fine old church with a tall spire crowns the town.

The entry gives a town count of more than seventeen thousand souls. It notes twin old libraries kept safe inside the church. A famed school in the town taught the great thinker Isaac Newton as a boy. A bronze statue in the town marks that link for all to see. An inn from the fifteenth century and a stone conduit in the market place are also named.
britannica-1911-hamilton-william:
William Hamilton (1704–1754) was a Scottish poet. He wrote the well-known song The Braes of Yarrow. He was born at Bangour in Linlithgowshire. His father was a member of the Scottish bar. By 1724 he was contributing to Allan Ramsay's Tea Table Miscellany. In 1745 he joined Prince Charles' cause. He celebrated Prestonpans in verse, though he may not have borne arms.

After Culloden he hid for months in the Highlands. He escaped to France, then won leave to return in 1749. The family estate of Bangour came to him in 1750. Poor health forced him to live abroad again. He died at Lyons on 25 March 1754. His poems are odes, songs, epitaphs and translations. None but The Braes of Yarrow shows striking originality. Adam Smith prefaced the first, unauthorised edition of 1748.
britannica-1911-harrison-william:
William Harrison lived from 1534 to 1593 and wrote on the land of England. The 1911 Britannica life calls him a topographer and a man of old lore.
