He was born in London in April 1534, the entry notes. He was schooled at St Paul's and at Westminster in his youth. In 1551 he went up to Cambridge for his studies there.

He took his degree from Christ Church at Oxford in 1560. By then he was rector of Radwinter in Essex from 1559. From 1571 he held a second living at Wimbish in that county. In 1586 he became a canon of Windsor in the royal chapel. His famed Description of England grew from a vast planned work.
britannica-1911-hart-william:
William Hart was an American landscape and cattle painter of Scottish birth. He lived from eighteen twenty three to eighteen ninety four. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paisley, he was taken to America in early youth.

Hart trained as a carriage painter at Albany in New York state. His first art work was landscape scenes on coach side panels. He went back to Scotland for three years of study after that. In eighteen fifty three he opened a studio in New York city. As part of the Hudson River School he won wide public favour. His works hang in many well known American collections of art.
britannica-1911-haughton-william:
William Haughton (fl. 1598) was an English playwright. Almost nothing certain is known of his life. He collaborated with Chettle, Dekker, Day and Hathway. Philip Henslowe's diary preserves the one firm fact. On 10 March 1600 Henslowe lent him ten shillings. The loan freed Haughton from the Clink prison. Mr Fleay credits him with a large share in The Patient Grissill (1599).

English-Men for my Money (1598) is ascribed to him alone. Its full title adds A Woman will have her Will. The Devil and his Dame was announced by Henslowe in 1600. Fleay identifies it with Grim, the Collier of Croydon. That play sends a devil's emissary to report on married life. It was printed in 1662. Both plays survive in Hazlitt's edition of Dodsley's Old Plays.
britannica-1911-hawes-william:
William Hawes (1785–1846) was an English musician born in London. For eight years he sang as a Chapel Royal chorister. Dr Ayrton taught him music there. In 1817 he became master of the Chapel Royal children. He also ran a music publishing business. For many years he directed music at the Lyceum theatre. That house was then devoted to English opera.

On 23 July 1824 he introduced Weber's Der Freischütz to England. The production came first curtailed, then complete. Mozart's Così fan tutte followed under his auspices. Marschner's Vampyre also reached the stage through him. He wrote or compiled music for numerous pieces. His glees and madrigals were better than his stage music. Several collections of them were published. He superintended a new edition of The Triumph of Oriana. He died on 18 February 1846.
britannica-1911-hayley-william:
William Hayley (1745–1820) was an English writer. He was born at Chichester on 9 November 1745. Eton and Trinity Hall, Cambridge, educated him. Private means let him retire to Eartham in Sussex in 1774. Occasional poems filled his early years. Garrick rejected his tragedy The Afflicted Father in 1771. Colman declined his Syrian Queen the same year. Poetical essays and epistles won his real fame.

His Triumphs of Temper (1781) ran to twelve or fourteen editions. Byron later ridiculed it in English Bards. On Warton's death in 1790 Hayley refused the laureateship. His Life of Milton appeared in 1794. Cowper's friendship began in 1792 and lasted till 1800. Hayley helped win Cowper his pension. He introduced William Blake to Flaxman. His biography of Cowper crowns his later reputation.
britannica-1911-hayward-abraham:
Abraham Hayward (1801–1884) was an English man of letters. He was born at Wilton, near Salisbury, on 22 November 1801. Blundell's school, Tiverton, educated him. The Inner Temple called him to the bar in 1832. He had edited the Law Magazine since 1829. That editorship connected him with Austin, Lewis and Savigny. He translated Savigny's tractate into English. In 1833 he printed a prose Faust translation privately.

Carlyle called that Faust the best version of its time. Reviewing became Hayward's real career afterward. The Quarterly and Edinburgh reviews took his essays. Articles on gastronomy in 1835–1836 were his first successes. The Art of Dining (1852) reprinted them. The Athenaeum Club elected him in 1835. For nearly fifty years he was among its most influential members. His Goethe volume for Blackwood appeared in 1878. His correspondence filled two volumes after death.
britannica-1911-hazlitt-william:
William Hazlitt (1778–1830) was a British literary critic and essayist. He was born at Maidstone on 10 April 1778. His father was a Unitarian minister there. The family migrated to America in 1783. They returned in 1787 and settled at Wem in Shropshire. Hackney theological college was meant to make him a minister. Hazlitt had no inclination for that career. Portrait painting was his next ambition, from 1802.

Coleridge's 1798 visit to Shrewsbury changed his inner life. He heard Coleridge preach and caught fire for metaphysics. Nether Stowey brought him Wordsworth's acquaintance too. Charles Lamb became a close London friend. Paris in 1802 gave him four happy months copying Louvre portraits. Painting slowly yielded to writing in his life. The long account follows his essays, lectures and feuds. His Literary Remains preserved the Coleridge memoir. Family papers and Stephen's essay close the bibliography.
britannica-1911-herbert-henry-william:
Henry William Herbert (1807–1858) was an English novelist and writer on sport who used the pen name Frank Forester. Born in London on the 3rd of April 1807, a son of the dean of Manchester, he was schooled at Eton and Caius College, Cambridge. Fallen into debt, he emigrated to America. From 1831 to 1839 he taught Greek in a New York school.

In 1833 he started the American Monthly Magazine. His first novel, The Brothers: a Tale of the Fronde, came out in 1834. More novels and studies of cavaliers, knights and captains followed. His name rests on sport: The Field Sports of the United States and British Provinces (1849) and The Fish and Fishing of the United States (1850). His last big work was The Horse and Horsemanship in the United States (1858). He also translated many novels of Sue and Dumas. He died by his own hand in New York on the 17th of May 1858.
britannica-1911-heysham:
Heysham is a seaport in the Lancaster parliamentary division of Lancashire, England, on the south shore of Morecambe Bay, served by the Midland railway. Its population was 3,381 in 1901. Under powers got from parliament in 1896, the Midland Railway Company built a harbour enclosed by breakwaters, opened in 1904. It was made to grow traffic with Belfast and other Irish ports, and a daily first-class passenger service to Belfast was set up.

The harbour has a depth at low tide of 17 ft., with wide room for livestock and goods of all kinds. Heysham is also somewhat in favour as a watering-place. St Peter's church is mainly Norman, with fragments of even earlier date. Near it stand the ruins of a very old oratory, dedicated to St Patrick. Tradition says it was raised as a place of prayer for those at sea.
britannica-1911-hicks-william:
William Hicks (1830–1883) was a British soldier who entered the Bombay army in 1849. He served through the Indian mutiny and was praised in despatches for Sitka Ghaut in 1859. In the Abyssinian expedition of 1867–1868 he was a brigade major. He retired as honorary colonel in 1880, and after the Egyptian war of 1882 he entered the khedive's service as a pasha.

Early in 1883 Hicks went to Khartum as chief of staff and beat a dervish force in Sennar. Court intrigue turned on him, yet he was made commander of an expedition to crush the mahdi in Kordofan. He warned that his force was worthless for the task. The march began on the 9th of September: 7,000 infantry, 1,000 cavalry and 2,000 followers. Misled by treacherous guides and stricken with thirst, the army was ambushed at Kashgil on the 5th of November. All but some 300 men were killed, Hicks last of all.
britannica-1911-hilton-william:
William Hilton is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Hilton was an English painter who lived from 1786 to 1839. He was born in Lincoln, son of a portrait painter. In 1800 he was placed with an engraver to learn the trade. At the same time he began study at the Royal Academy school. He first showed work there in 1803.

The article says he soon won a name for choice of subject and for design and colour. He toured Italy with a fellow painter. In 1813 he was elected an associate of the Academy, and in 1820 a full member. His large work Christ Crowned with Thorns is called his masterpiece. In 1827 he became keeper of the Academy. The National Gallery holds several of his works. One shows Edith finding the body of Harold after battle.
britannica-1911-hingham:
Hingham is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a township in Massachusetts. It lies in Plymouth county on Massachusetts Bay. Counts put its people near five thousand at the time. Its area is about thirty square miles in all. A railway crosses the township from end to end. Hingham Center and South Hingham are also named. Derby Academy stands among its schools of note.

Sarah Derby founded and endowed that school in 1784. It opened in 1791 for boys and girls alike. The town has a public library dating from 1868. Its shelves held twelve thousand volumes by 1908. The Old Meeting House was raised in 1681. It is one of the oldest church buildings in the land. It has been in constant use since that year. Settlers came to the place as early as 1633. Many came from Hingham in Norfolk, which gave the name.
britannica-1911-hogarth-william:
William Hogarth (1697–1764) was the great English painter and pictorial satirist, born at Bartholomew Close in London in 1697. His father Richard, a schoolmaster and literary hack from Westmorland, died in 1718. The son showed early talent for drawing rather than school learning. By his own wish he was apprenticed to Ellis Gamble, a silver-plate engraver in Leicester Fields, and by April 1720 he was engraving on his own account.

Copper engraving was Hogarth's utmost ambition at twenty, and he set himself to learn drawing from memory of the things he saw. The long entry traces the career that grew from those beginnings. It closes by placing his works. The Election series is in the Soane Museum; the March to Finchley and Captain Coram are in the Foundling. The British Museum's Print Room holds his designs for Industry and Idleness, most of them once Horace Walpole's.
britannica-1911-hone-william:
William Hone (1780–1842) was an English writer and bookseller, born at Bath on the 3rd of June 1780. His father raised his children in sectarian narrowness, and Hone was taught to read from the Bible only. Placed in an attorney's office in 1790, he moved through solicitors' offices at Chatham and Gray's Inn. He disliked the law.

Hone married in 1800 and set up a book and print shop with a circulating library in Lambeth Walk. His first publication was Shaw's Gardener (1806). A plan with John Bone for popular savings banks failed, and a joint venture ended in bankruptcy. In 1811 the trade chose him as its auctioneer. His inquiries into lunatic asylums again wrecked his business. In 1815 he started the Traveller and fought in vain to clear Eliza Fenning, hanged for poisoning. In his last years he turned devout and preached at Weigh House Chapel.
britannica-1911-hopkins-william:
William Hopkins is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an English scholar of numbers and rocks. He lived from 1793 to 1866 in England. He was born in Nottinghamshire in February 1793. In youth he learned farm work in Norfolk. He then took a large farm in Suffolk and failed. At age thirty he entered Cambridge to study.

He took his first degree in 1827 with high rank. A book on angles and measures came out in 1833. He won fame as a tutor whose pupils did well. A trip with Sedgwick turned him to the study of rocks. He used numbers to probe how forces lift the crust. Work on the Lake District and the Weald came from that study. He wrote on glaciers and on stray blocks as well. Top honours in his field came to him in 1850.
britannica-1911-horsley-william:
William Horsley (1774–1858) was an English musician, born on 15 November 1774. In 1790 he became the pupil of Theodore Smith, a weak master of the time. Smith still taught him enough to win the post of organist at Ely Chapel, Holborn, in 1794. Horsley left that post in 1798 to be organist at the Asylum for Female Orphans. There he was helper to Dr Callcott, his close friend, whose eldest daughter he wed.

In 1802 Horsley took Callcott's place on the latter's move. He also became organist of Belgrave Chapel in 1812 and of the Charter House in 1838. He died on 12 June 1858. His works are many, and they include three symphonies for a full band. His glees hold far more weight in his name.
britannica-1911-hoste-sir-william:
Sir William Hoste (1780–1828) was a British naval captain, son of Dixon Hoste, rector of Godwick and Tittleshill in Norfolk. He was born on the 26th of August 1780 at Ingoldsthorpe, and entered the navy in April 1793 under Nelson's special care. He became lieutenant in 1798 and was given the Mutine brig after the battle of the Nile. In 1802 Lord St Vincent made him post captain.

Hoste's whole active career lay in the Mediterranean and Adriatic. From 1808 to 1814 he commanded a detached force of frigates against the French in Dalmatia and the Venetian squadron Napoleon had formed. The work was profitable too: captured merchant ships brought him at least £60,000. His most brilliant feat came on the 13th of March 1811 off Lissa. A Franco-Venetian force of six frigates and five small vessels attacked his four frigates in two lines, copying Nelson at Trafalgar. Hoste's fast handling and gunnery won the day.
britannica-1911-how-william-walsham:
William Walsham How (1823–1897) was an English divine, son of a Shrewsbury solicitor, born on the 13th of December 1823. He was educated at Shrewsbury school and Wadham College, Oxford, and ordained in 1846. For over thirty years he worked in parishes at Whittington in Shropshire and at Oswestry, where he was rural dean from 1860. He refused promotion several times.

His energy made How known far beyond his parish. In 1879 he became a suffragan bishop in London, as bishop of Bedford, with the East End as his field. There he inspired a revival of church work, founded the East London Church Fund, and gathered a large band of helpers. His love of children earned him the name of the children's bishop. In 1888 he became bishop of Wakefield, and did the same valued work in the north. He died in 1897, remembered also for hymns still sung.
britannica-1911-howard-lord-william:
Lord William Howard (1563–1640), known as Belted, or Bauld, Will, was the third son of Thomas Howard, 4th duke of Norfolk, who was executed in 1572. He was born at Audley End in Essex on the 19th of December 1563. In 1577 he married Elizabeth, daughter of Thomas, Lord Dacre, and later went to Cambridge. Suspected of treason with his elder brother Philip, earl of Arundel, he was imprisoned in 1583, 1585 and 1589.

Howard joined the church of Rome in 1584. Both brothers lost part of their Dacre estates under Elizabeth, restored in 1601 for a payment of £10,000. Howard then settled with his children and grandchildren at Naworth Castle in Cumberland. He rebuilt the castle, improved the estate and set order in that border country. The account follows his long life there after 1603, the library he gathered, and the stern local rule that made Belted Will a legend of the north.
britannica-1911-huggins-sir-william:
Sir William Huggins is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an English star scholar from 1824 to 1910. He was born in London in February 1824. He was taught at a city school and by home tutors. He chose to give his life to the study of stars. In 1856 he built his own viewing house in south London. At first he did plain routine work on the skies.

New work on light splits soon drew his full zeal. He turned to the stuff that stars are made of. First fruits of that work came in the year 1863. He worked with a partner on lines of fixed stars. Trials with photos of star spectra came the same year. In 1875 he took up dry plates for the task. Long light spells then laid bare stars too faint to see.
britannica-1911-hulme-william:
William Hulme (1631-1691) was an English giver to good causes, born near Manchester. He died on 29 October 1691. He had lost his only son, Banastre. Hulme left his wealth in trust to keep four poor scholars for four years at Brasenose College, Oxford. That gift was the start of the Hulme Trust. Its lands lay in Manchester, and their worth grew fast with the town.

In 1881 the charity commissioners drew up a scheme for the trust, and that scheme, as changed in 1907, still rules it. Its income of about 10,000 pounds a year keeps up the Hulme Grammar School in Manchester. It also aids other schools and backs a college of religion, Hulme Hall, tied to the university of Manchester. It gives a number of grants and awards at Brasenose College as well.
britannica-1911-hunter-william:
William Hunter, a British doctor who lived from 1718 to 1783, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is called the first great teacher of anatomy in England. Born in Lanark, he first meant to join the church. Doubts on church tests led him to choose medicine on the advice of his friend William Cullen.

Hunter trained at Glasgow, Edinburgh, and London in turn. In London he worked as a dissector for a noted anatomist and as a pupil at Saint Georges Hospital. When his patron died, he stayed on with the family. In 1746 he began talks on surgery for a group of naval doctors. The talks went so well that anatomy was added to the course. His fame as a teacher grew fast, for his courses were full and his models were the best of their day.
britannica-1911-ince-william:
William Ince was an English furniture designer and cabinetmaker of the 18th century. He was one of the most successful followers of Chippendale, though his work was in many ways lighter. His designs helped form a bridge between the heavy, rich style of Chippendale and the slighter forms of Hepplewhite that followed.

Many of his designs were poor and overdone, but his best work was very good. His chairs are at times mistaken for Chippendale's work, though they fall well below it. He was drawn to the Chinese and Gothic tastes of the later 18th century. For many years he worked in partnership with Thomas Mayhew in Broad Street, Golden Square, London. Together they issued a folio of ninety-five plates, The Universal System of Household Furniture, with text in English and French, most likely about 1762.
britannica-1911-janssens-van-nuyssen-abr:
Abraham Janssens van Nuyssen is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Antwerp in 1567, he was a Flemish painter trained by Jan Snellinck. He became a master in 1602 and dean of the master painters in 1607.

The article rates him against his great peer Rubens. Till Rubens rose, Janssens was held to be the best painter of past scenes of his time. In sound drawing he beat Rubens, the text says. In bold design and in painting the nude form he matched him. But in colour and free touch he fell well short. His skill with light and shade shows in torch lit scenes. Fine works hang at Antwerp and Vienna.
britannica-1911-jenner-sir-william:
Sir William Jenner, an English physician who lived from 1815 to 1898, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Chatham, he was educated at University College in London and qualified in surgery and in the college of physicians. In 1847 he began work at the London fever hospital on cases of continued fever.

That work let Jenner draw at last the distinction between typhus and typhoid, and his reputation as a pathologist rests chiefly on it. In 1849 he was appointed professor of pathological anatomy at University College, and he rose to physician at its hospital. He held two more chairs there as well. He was president of the college of physicians from 1881 to 1888. In 1861 he became a physician to Queen Victoria, and he attended both the prince consort and the prince of Wales in their attacks of typhoid.
britannica-1911-jerrold-douglas-william:
Douglas William Jerrold, an English dramatist and man of letters, was born in London in eighteen o three. His father Samuel was an actor who ran a small theatre in Kent. In eighteen o seven the family moved to Sheerness, a port town. There Douglas grew up among the sailors who crowded the port in wartime. He took a child's part on stage at times, but the stage drew him little.

In December eighteen thirteen Jerrold joined a guardship as a midshipman. He served until the peace of eighteen fifteen closed the war. That peace ruined his father, since prize money ended with it. The family moved to London in eighteen sixteen to start again. Douglas became a printer's apprentice, then a compositor on a Sunday paper. Small papers and verses by him had already appeared in cheap magazines.
britannica-1911-johnson-sir-william:
Sir William Johnson (1715–1774), British soldier and American pioneer, was born in County Meath, Ireland, the son of a country gentleman. Trained for trade, he crossed to America in 1738 to manage land in the Mohawk Valley, New York, that belonged to his uncle, Admiral Sir Peter Warren. His settlement prospered, and he built a rich trade with the Indians.

The Mohawks adopted him and made him a sachem. In 1744 he became superintendent of the affairs of the Six Nations, and he raised them for war with French Canada. Made a general in 1755, he beat the French and their allies at Lake George that September and was wounded. Parliament thanked him and he was made a baronet. From 1756 until his death he was sole superintendent of the northern Indians. He served in the failed attack on Ticonderoga in 1758, then took chief command at Fort Niagara in 1759 and captured the fort.
britannica-1911-jones-william:
William Jones, an English divine born at Lowick in seventeen twenty six, came from an old Welsh family. One of his forebears was Colonel John Jones, a brother in law of Cromwell. Jones was schooled at Charterhouse and at University College, Oxford. There a shared love of music drew him close to George Horne. Horne later became bishop of Norwich, and Jones wrote his life.

After his degree in seventeen forty nine, Jones held a string of church posts. In seventeen seventy seven he took the curacy of Nayland in Suffolk. His home there became a centre for High Church friends. He was a link between the old non jurors and the later Oxford movement. His tract on the Trinity came out in seventeen fifty six.
britannica-1911-kaye-sir-john-william:
Sir John William Kaye (1814–1876) was an English military historian, son of Charles Kaye, a solicitor. He was schooled at Eton and at the Royal Military College, Addiscombe. From 1832 to 1841 he served as an officer in the Bengal Artillery, and then spent some years in literary work in India and in England.

In 1856 he entered the civil service of the East India Company. When the government of India passed to the crown, he followed John Stuart Mill as secretary of the political and secret department of the India Office. He was made a K.C.S.I. in 1871 and died in London on the 24th of July 1876. His many writings include the History of the Sepoy War in India, issued from 1864 to 1876. He also wrote a History of the War in Afghanistan and a study of the Administration of the East India Company.
britannica-1911-kidd-william:
William Kidd, Captain Kidd (about 1645 to 1701), was a privateer and pirate, and this 1911 Britannica entry opens with what little is sure of his start. He was perhaps born in Greenock, Scotland, but his origin is quite obscure. He told the Newgate chaplain that he was about fifty-six when condemned for piracy in 1701. In 1691 the council of New York gave him a money award for his services in the troubles after the revolution of 1688.

He owned ships of his own and served with credit against the French in the West Indies. In 1695 he came to London with his own sloop. A New York landowner named Livingston named him to Lord Bellomont as the man to command against the pirates of the eastern seas. The Adventure Galley, of thirty guns, was fitted out in private hands, and Kidd got the king's commission to seize pirates.
britannica-1911-kingsford-william:
William Kingsford, a British engineer and Canadian historian who lived from 1819 to 1898, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in London in December 1819. He first read architecture, but the life of an office irked him and he joined the Dragoon Guards. He got his discharge in Canada in 1841.

He worked in the office of the city surveyor of Montreal and made a survey for the Lachine canal. He then built rail works in the United States and in Panama. From 1853 he served the Grand Trunk railroad as surveyor and district chief till 1864. From 1872 to 1879 he held a state post in charge of the harbours of the Great Lakes. In 1880 he took to the records of Canada at Ottawa. His great work was a History of Canada in ten volumes, from 1887 to 1897.
britannica-1911-kirkcaldy-of-grange-sir-:
Sir William Kirkcaldy of Grange (c. 1520–1573) was a Scottish politician, eldest son of Sir James Kirkcaldy of Grange, of an old Fifeshire family. Sir James was lord high treasurer of Scotland from 1537 to 1543 and a firm opponent of Cardinal Beaton, for whose murder in 1546 he was partly to blame.

William helped to bring about that murder. When the castle of St Andrews gave up to the French in July 1547, he was sent as a prisoner to Normandy, from which he escaped in 1550. He then served in France as a secret agent for the advisers of Edward VI, known in the ciphers as Corax. Later he served in the French army, where he won a lasting name for skill and courage. The sentence for his share in Beaton's murder was lifted in 1556. Coming back to Scotland in 1557, he rose fast to the front as a leader of the Protestant lords.
britannica-1911-kurram:
Kurram is a river and district on the Kohat border of the North-West Frontier province of India. The river drains the south flanks of the Safed Koh, reaches the plains above Bannu, and joins the Indus near Isa-Khel after more than 200 miles. The district covers 1278 square miles and held 54,257 people in 1901. It is well watered and thick with small fortified villages, orchards and groves,. Its people, the Turis, are of Turki origin.

The valley once answered to Kabul, which sent troops every few years to gather the revenue by force. The Turis, being Shiah Muslims, disliked Afghan rule. In the second Afghan War they gave Sir Frederick Roberts every help as he advanced by the Peiwar Kotal, and in 1880 their independence was granted. In 1890, at their own request, the British took over the running of the valley, as an agency rather than a district.
britannica-1911-kuttalam:
Kuttalam, or Courtallum, is a health resort of southern India, in the Tinnevelly district of Madras. In 1901 it held 1197 people. It stands only 450 feet above the sea, yet it has the climate of a far higher place. Breezes reach it through a gap in the Ghats, and cool it.

The place has long been a favourite resort for European visitors. Its season runs from July to September. A new railway, from Tinnevelly into Travancore, has lately made it easier to reach. The scenery around it is most picturesque, and it has a waterfall of great fame in the district.
britannica-1911-laidlaw-william:
William Laidlaw (1780–1845), friend and amanuensis of Sir Walter Scott, was born at Blackhouse in Selkirkshire on the 19th of November 1780, the son of a sheep farmer. After a simple schooling at Peebles he went back to work on his father's farm. James Hogg, the shepherd poet, worked at Blackhouse for some years and became Laidlaw's friend and appreciative critic. Together they helped Scott by supplying material for his Border Minstrelsy.

After two failures as a farmer in Midlothian and Peebleshire, Laidlaw became Scott's steward at Abbotsford. He also served as Scott's amanuensis at different times, taking down from dictation a large part of The Bride of Lammermoor, The Legend of Montrose and Ivanhoe. He died at Contin near Dingwall on the 18th of May 1845. Of his own poetry little is known beyond Lucy's Flittin', printed in Hogg's Forest Minstrel.
britannica-1911-lane-edward-william:
Edward William Lane is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English scholar of Arabic born in eighteen hundred and one. Poor health ended his first trade, so he sailed for Egypt in eighteen twenty five. He spent three years there and drew and wrote a full account.

The entry tells how he lived in Cairo as a local scholar to learn daily life. His book on the modern people of Egypt won instant and lasting praise. He then gave English readers a famed version of the Arabian Nights tales. Rich notes on custom and faith fill that work. He spent his last great years building a vast word book of Arabic.
britannica-1911-langland-william:
William Langland (about 1332 to about 1400) is named in the 1911 Britannica as the supposed single poet behind Piers the Plowman, the great poem of the 1300s. Nothing firm is known of his life apart from what the copies of the poem and its own lines suggest, so the account deals first with the text itself.

Three forms survive, called the A, B, and C texts, held in ten, fourteen, and seventeen copies, with seven more of mixed type. The A text runs to 2,567 lines, the B text to 7,242, and the C text, a reworking of B, to 7,357. Crowley printed the B text three times in 1550. Later pages weigh who wrote which form, and whether one hand made them all.
britannica-1911-lauder-william:
William Lauder (died 1771) was a Scottish scholar remembered as a literary forger, and his rise and fall are told in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Educated at Edinburgh, he failed to win posts there and came to London in 1742. He was a good scholar, and in 1739 he published a set of sacred Latin poems by Scottish writers.

The entry centers on his claim, from 1747, that Milton's Paradise Lost was largely stolen from older poets. Scholars soon proved he had garbled his quotes and even slipped in lines from a Latin version of Paradise Lost itself. Exposed, he confessed at the dictation of Samuel Johnson, then left for Barbados, where he died.
britannica-1911-lilly-william:
William Lilly (1602-1681) was an English reader of the stars. Diseworth in Leicestershire was his birthplace. His yeoman kin had sat there for ages. School at Ashby-de-la-Zouche gave him a fair grounding in Latin. His master, he notes, never taught him logic.

Want drove him to London at eighteen. He served an old citizen and his wife. The master's death in 1627 left him a small yearly sum. Marriage to the widow came next. Her death in 1633 left him goods worth some £1000. Star books then filled his days. Years 1642 and 1643 went to deep study, above all of Naibod. War acts of king and parliament drew his eye. He framed a method and held to it for life. Yearly forecasts and kindred works made his name with men of the Long Parliament.
britannica-1911-lilye-william:
William Lilye (about 1468-1522) was an English scholar born at Odiham in Hampshire. Oxford took him in 1486. A pilgrimage to Jerusalem followed his arts degree. Rhodes, Rome, and Venice fed his learning on the way home. Greek exiles and famed teachers shaped him in those years.

Back in London he taught grammar on his own. Men hold him the first to teach Greek in that city. Thomas More grew close to him. In 1510 Dean Colet set him as first high master of the new St Paul's School. Plague killed him on 25 February 1522. His lasting mark is a shared book, the old Latin grammar used at Eton for ages. Two parts are surely his: verses on noun genders and on verb forms. Latin prose and verse of his own also survive.
britannica-1911-livingston-william:
William Livingston, who lived from 1723 to 1790, was an American political leader. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Albany, New York. He came of the great Livingston Manor house on the Hudson. His grandfather had founded that family in America. William graduated at Yale in 1741 and read law in New York. He joined the bar in 1748 and sat in the legislature.

His real sway ran through print, not office. In 1752 he founded the Independent Reflector, a weekly paper. In its columns he fought the Anglican bid to seize King's College. His family led the Whig side in the colony's feuds. The De Lanceys led the Tory side against them. After the Reflector was shut, he ran the Watch Tower in another paper. That sheet became the voice of the Presbyterian faction.
britannica-1911-longchamp-william:
William Longchamp, who died in 1197, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He served as chancellor of England and as bishop of Ely. He entered public life late in the reign of Henry the Second, as an aide to the king's son Geoffrey, though Henry disliked him and called him the son of two traitors.

Longchamp soon left Geoffrey for Richard and won trust as a skilled envoy, besting Henry's peace bid at Paris in 1189. When Richard took the throne, William became chancellor and bishop, and when the king left England he shared the top rule of the realm. He pushed his fellow ruler out within months and gained a papal legate's powers too. But pride, scorn for the English, and tours with a train of a thousand knights made him hated. Even Prince John looked like the better choice.
britannica-1911-lytham:
Lytham is a seaside town in Lancashire, England, and this short 1911 Britannica entry describes it briefly. It stands on the north shore of the Ribble estuary, west of Preston, on a joint railway line. Its people numbered 7,185 in 1901. It has a pier, a pleasant promenade, and a drive along the shore, with the other marks of a watering place.

Yet the entry notes that Lytham is less given over to holiday crowds than Blackpool, which lies eight miles to the north-west. A Benedictine cell was founded at Lytham at the close of the twelfth century by the lord of the manor, Richard Fitz-Roger.
britannica-1911-maccormac-sir-william:
Sir William MacCormac (1836-1901) was an Irish surgeon who made his name in London. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his study at Belfast, Dublin, and Paris. He began work in Belfast, then moved to London in 1861. War service soon shaped his skill and his fame.

He led ambulance work in the Franco German war and was at Sedan. That work made him a known expert on gunshot wounds. At Saint Thomas Hospital he served for twenty years as surgeon and teacher. He led the Royal College of Surgeons for five straight years. In South Africa he advised the forces as a consulting surgeon.
britannica-1911-maclure-william:
William Maclure lived from 1763 to 1840 and was a geologist of America. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Ayr in Scotland, his birth town. After a short trip to New York in 1782, he joined a London firm. That house traded with American merchants across the sea in goods. In 1796 his work took him to Virginia, which became his home.

A post on claims from France sent him to Europe in 1803. Those years abroad lit a deep love of geology in him. Back home in 1807 he set himself a vast lone task. He would survey the rocks of the whole United States alone. He crossed the Alleghany range some fifty times in that work.
britannica-1911-magee-william:
William Magee (1766–1831) was archbishop of Dublin, born at Enniskillen and schooled at Trinity College, Dublin. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his rise from fellow in 1788 to ordination in 1790. Two college sermons grew into his Discourses on the Scriptural Doctrines of Atonement and Sacrifice in 1801, an attack on Unitarian teaching.

He gave up a chair of mathematics and college posts in 1812 to take country livings, then became dean of Cork in 1813. Known as a preacher and a driver of the Irish reformation, he was made bishop of Raphoe in 1819. In 1822 he stepped up to Dublin as archbishop. A tolerant man in most things, he still fought Catholic Emancipation to the end. He died on the 18th of August 1831.
britannica-1911-maginn-william:
William Maginn was an Irish poet and press writer born at Cork in the late seventeen hundreds. Son of a schoolmaster, he finished at Trinity College in Dublin and took over his fathers school on his death. He then began to write for leading papers and for a famed Scots monthly, under false names.

The 1911 Britannica entry credits him with first making his mark as a maker of comic copies and witty Latin verse. He is said to have thought up a famed set of night talks for the monthly, and wrote some of its best parts. His tie to that paper lasted near his whole life. In London he worked on short lived papers, but drink and loose conduct in press work blocked firm success.
britannica-1911-maitland-frederic-willia:
Frederic William Maitland, a giant of English law lore, fills a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1850, he was schooled at Eton and Trinity, Cambridge. He topped the moral sciences list there in the year 1872. A prize for world law work came to him at that time. Called to the bar in 1876, he learned equity law in depth.

In time Maitland gave his life to the past of English law. In 1884 Cambridge made him reader in that deep field. Four years on he held the Downing chair of English laws. Ill health dogged his last years, yet his fame kept growing. He brought out plea rolls and court books for the Selden Society. His History of English Law, writ with Pollock, capped the work.
britannica-1911-markby-sir-william:
Markby, Sir William is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English jurist. Born at Duxford in 1829, the rector's fourth son, he was educated at Bury St Edmunds and Merton College, Oxford. He was called to the bar in 1856 and became recorder of Buckingham in 1865. In 1866 he went to India as a judge of the High Court of Calcutta, a post he held for twelve years.

The article then follows his work as a legal writer in England. On retiring he became Reader in Indian Law at Oxford. Beside lectures on Indian law, he wrote the Elements of Law, a book on the general principles of jurisprudence first meant for Indian students. The article praises it for facing hard questions of definition that most textbooks pass over.
britannica-1911-martin-william:
William Martin, an English naturalist who lived from 1767 to 1810, is the subject of a brief 1911 Britannica article. He was the son of a hosier and was born at Mansfield in 1767. He learned drawing as a boy from James Bolton at Halifax. From Bolton he gained a taste for the study of nature.

In 1796 Martin was made a fellow of the Linnaean Society. In 1805 he took a post as drawing master at a grammar school in Macclesfield. He is best known for two early works on British fossils, both printed in 1809. One sets out the fossils found in Derbyshire with figures and accounts. The other seeks a science based plan for the study of such finds. He died at Macclesfield in 1810.
britannica-1911-mason-william:
William Mason is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an English poet who lived from 1725 to 1797. He was born in February 1725, the son of a vicar. He studied at Cambridge and took holy orders. In 1744 he wrote a lament for Pope. Through the help of Thomas Gray he won a college post. He became a close friend of Gray for life.

Gray shaped his verse and curbed its worst faults. A poem of 1748 hit at Oxford and drew a sharp reply. Two plays tried to wed new drama to old Greek forms. Both plays were cold works meant more to be read. Friends gave split views on their worth at the time. When Gray died he left Mason in charge of his works. A life of Gray from his hand came out in 1774.
britannica-1911-may-william:
William May was an English churchman of the sixteen hundreds era of reform, brother to a bishop of Carlisle. Schooled at Cambridge, he was a fellow of one hall there and then head of a college. He backed the break with Rome with warmth.

The 1911 Britannica entry lists his string of church posts in the diocese of Ely, as clerk, deputy, and canon in turn. He rose to a canon post at a great London church, then to its dean. His kind report on the colleges of Cambridge saved them from being dissolved by the crown. Cast out under a Catholic queen, he was restored when a new queen took the throne. He died on the very day he was picked for a great northern archbishop post.
britannica-1911-mccombie-william:
William McCombie, a Scottish farm man born in eighteen hundred and five, is covered in a short entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Tillyfour in Aberdeenshire, he founded the herd of black polled cattle that bears his name. That herd is the core fact of his fame. The entry is brief, but each line adds a firm point.

He was the first tenant farmer to sit for a Scottish seat in Parliament. The west division of Aberdeen sent him there with no foe in the field in eighteen sixty eight. He died with no wife in February of eighteen eighty. His book on cattle and cattle breeders came out in eighteen sixty seven. It ran to a fourth run in eighteen eighty six. The note suits readers who track farm breed lore or first steps for farm men in high office.
britannica-1911-meade-william:
William Meade lived from 1789 to 1862 and was an American Episcopal bishop. The 1911 Britannica life makes him son of Richard Kidder Meade. That father had served as an aide to General Washington in war. William was born near Millwood in Virginia in November 1789. He graduated first in his class at Princeton in the year 1808.

He studied theology in Maryland and at Princeton after his degree. He was ordained deacon in 1811 and priest three years later. For a time he preached at Millwood and at Alexandria in turn. In 1829 he became assistant bishop of the state of Virginia. In 1841 he rose to bishop of Virginia in his own right.
britannica-1911-menam:
Menam, or Me Nam, is the main river of Siam. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica renders its name as mother water or main river. Yearly rise and fall of its flood sets the rice crop below. It starts high in the Nan hills as a small stream.

Names shift as it runs: Nam Nan, Nam, then Menam Pichai in turn. Deep swamp basins catch its flood on the lower plain in rains. Fish by the thousands of tons are cured as waters fall. Teak floats down its branches to the duty post at Paknam Po. Past Ayuthia the rich heart of Siam spreads along its banks.
britannica-1911-mignon-abraham:
Mignon, Abraham, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Dutch painter. Born at Frankfort in 1640, he was the son of a merchant. His father placed him with Jacob Merrel, a still-life painter. Merrel took him to Holland about the year 1660.

He then worked under de Heem at Utrecht, a famed hand at the craft. In 1675 he wed the daughter of the painter Cornelis Willaerts. Sibylle Merian, a pupil of his, won fame as a flower painter herself. Mignon gave his art almost wholly to flowers, fruit, and birds. His best scheme set red or white roses at the heart of a dark ground. Dresden holds fifteen of his works.
britannica-1911-minto-william:
William Minto, who lived from 1845 to 1893, was a Scottish man of letters. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his books on English writing. He was born at Auchintoul in Aberdeenshire in October 1845. Aberdeen University trained him, with a year spent at Oxford.

Minto aided a professor at Aberdeen for some years. From 1874 to 1878 he edited a London review paper. In 1880 he took the full chair of logic and English at Aberdeen. His guide to English prose came out in 1872 to praise. A study of English poets from Chaucer onward followed it. Sound judgment and warm sympathy marked both of those works. He also wrote a life of Defoe and three slight novels. Many pieces by him fill the ninth edition of this very work.
britannica-1911-mohler-johann-adam:
Johann Adam Mohler is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Igersheim in Wurttemberg on the sixth of May 1796, he was a German writer on church doctrine. He entered the university at Tubingen in 1817 and was ordained a priest in 1819.

The article follows his teaching career at Tubingen and Munich. His lectures drew large crowds, with many Protestants among them. His chief book came out in 1832 and set the teachings of the two churches side by side. That book stirred sharp debate, and three strong replies came within two years. The rows it caused helped drive him to a chair at Munich in 1835. He died on the twelfth of April 1838, soon after a new post came his way.
britannica-1911-molesworth-sir-william:
Sir William Molesworth lived from 1810 to 1855 and was an English politician. The Britannica life of 1911 opens in London, where he was born. Son of the seventh baronet, he took that title in 1823. At Cambridge he fought a duel with his tutor, the entry says. A spell of study abroad followed that wild start to life.

When the Reform Act passed in 1832, he won a seat in Parliament. He sat for east Cornwall to back the ministry of Lord Grey. Through Charles Buller he met Grote and James Mill in London. In 1835 he helped found the London Review as a radical voice. He later bought the Westminster Review and merged the two journals.
britannica-1911-moorcroft-william:
William Moorcroft, an English rover born about seventeen seventy, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Lancashire, he was trained as a surgeon in Liverpool. On the end of that course he chose a new path. He gave himself to the care of sick beasts, studied that art in France, and set up in London.

He put out a tract on the care of sick horses, with a note for India. He then wrote a brief book on how to shoe a horse. A great trade firm in India gave him charge of their horse stud in Bengal. He left England for India in eighteen hundred and eight. Under his care the stud rose fast in grade. To make the breed yet more fine, he chose to trek into Central Asia for Turkoman horses. He took goods with him to open trade ties as well.
britannica-1911-morris-william:
Morris, William is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English poet and artist. William Morris was born at Walthamstow on the twenty-fourth of March 1834 and died in 1896. He was the third child of a London discount broker from Worcester. As a small boy he was frail but keen on books, and by age four he knew most of the Waverley novels well.

When he was six the family moved to Woodford Hall. The out-of-door life there made him strong. He rode in Epping Forest, at times in a toy suit of armour, and grew a close watcher of wild life, able to name any bird on the wing. He still read all that came his way. The tales of the Arabian Nights drew him most, along with the plant drawings in Gerard's Herbal.
britannica-1911-motherwell-william:
William Motherwell (1797-1835), a Scottish poet and collector of old songs, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Glasgow, the son of an ironmonger, he was bound at fifteen to work in a sheriff clerk's office at Paisley. In 1819 he became deputy clerk there. His spare hours went on gathering matter for a book of local ballads.

The article lists his books and posts. The Harp of Renfrewshire came out in 1819, and a larger gathering of old and new minstrelsy in 1827, with a fine essay on the history of the ballad at its head. His best known poems are named, among them Jeanie Morrison. He edited a Paisley newspaper from 1828 and a Glasgow one from 1830. A small book of his poems came out in 1832, and a larger one with his life story after his death.
britannica-1911-mulready-william:
William Mulready (1786-1863) was an English painter of scenes from daily life, born at Ennis in County Clare. This 1911 Britannica article follows him from a childhood move to London, where he drew from an early age. He entered the Academy schools in 1800 and won the silver palette of the Society of Arts two years later.

Mulready worked with the drawing master John Varley, whose sister he married, and tried many kinds of work. He painted portraits, taught drawing, and drew for cheap books for children up to 1809. He then found his gift for scene painting, shown in works such as the Carpenter's Shop of 1809 and the Barber's Shop of 1811, both shaped by the example of Wilkie.
britannica-1911-murdock-william:
William Murdock, who lived from 1754 to 1839, was a British inventor. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica credits him with gas light. He was born near Auchinleck in Ayrshire in August 1754. His father was a millwright and miller, and raised him to the trade.

In 1777 Murdock joined Boulton and Watt at their Soho works. He soon went to Cornwall to fit Watt engines there. Trials with coal gas there led toward a breakthrough. By 1802 part of the Soho factory shone with gas light. Inside use followed the next year as methods improved. He also devised a swaying engine and a long slide valve. A steam carriage in 1786 irked his famous employers at times. He is thought the true mind behind a Watt patent motion.
britannica-1911-murimuth-adam:
Adam Murimuth was an English churchman and chronicler of the fourteenth century. He lived from about twelve seventy four to thirteen forty seven. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in twelve seventy four or five, he studied civil law at Oxford.

Murimuth practised in the papal court at Avignon from thirteen twelve to thirteen eighteen. Edward the Second and Archbishop Winchelsey ranked among his clients then. Legal work won him canon posts at Hereford and Saint Paul churches. In thirteen thirty one he retired to a country living at Wraysbury. There he wrote the past of his own times from thirteen o three.
britannica-1911-negapatam:
Negapatam, a seaport of British India, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the Tanjore district of Madras and forms one town with Nagore, a port three miles north. Its people numbered 57,190 in 1901. It carries on a brisk trade with the Straits Settlements and Ceylon, with steamers running once a week to Colombo. Rice is its chief export.

The article notes its rail workshops and its depot for workers bound overseas as coolies. The town was one of the earliest Portuguese settlements on that coast. The Dutch took it in 1660 and made it their chief holding in India. The English took it in 1781, and for near fifty years it headed the district. A large body of Muslim traders of mixed Arab descent lives there, and two missions work in the town.
britannica-1911-north-walsham:
North Walsham is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a market town in Norfolk, England. It stands one hundred and thirty-one miles north-east of London, by rail. The count of 1901 gave its urban district 3,981 people. It lies in a farming district near the river Ant, a stream that feeds the Bure.

Its church of Saint Nicholas is a fine late Gothic building in the flint work of the district. It has a fine south porch and the ruin of a great west tower, part of which fell early in the eighteenth century. A grammar school was founded in 1606 and has since moved to new buildings. There is a market house of the sixteenth century. A good farm trade runs through the town, with cattle shows and fairs.
britannica-1911-nott-sir-william:
Sir William Nott, who lived from 1782 to 1845, was an English general, son of a Herefordshire farmer. The 1911 Britannica article says his father became an innkeeper at Carmarthen in 1794. Nott had thin schooling but won a cadetship in the Indian army. He sailed to India in 1800. By 1825 he led his own regiment of native foot. In 1838, at the start of the first Afghan war, he took command of a brigade.

Nott held Quetta through 1839 and took Khelat the next year. When Kabul rose in 1841 and the envoy was slain, orders came to quit Kandahar. Nott judged the orders void and held his post. He beat the foe near Kandahar and cleared the Baba Wali Pass. In 1842 he was told to leave by way of Kabul. On the march he routed the Afghans at Ghazni.
britannica-1911-nottingham:
Nottingham, a great midland city, is surveyed in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the north bank of the Trent and the Leen. Rail lines tie it to London and the north of England. Canals and the river give it trade routes by water too. In 1901 its folk came to just under two hundred and forty thousand.

A vast open market place spreads at the heart of the town. The entry calls it the largest of its kind in England. The castle crowns a steep rock hill to the south. Its old Norman gate still stands, restored for view. Since 1878 the castle has held an art museum for the midlands. Churches old and new, the piece notes, fill out the scene.
britannica-1911-oelschlager-adam:
Adam Oelschläger, also known as Olearius, was a German traveller and student of the East. A life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives his dates as 1600 to 1671. He studied at Leipzig and became librarian and court scholar to the duke of Holstein-Gottorp. In 1633 the duke made him secretary to an embassy to Muscovy and Persia.

The aim was a land route for silk that would end at the duke's new town. The party reached Moscow in 1634 and struck a good deal with the tsar. A second, longer trek took them down the Volga and across the Caspian Sea. They reached the Persian court at Isfahan in 1637, with less success there. On the way Oelschläger charted the Volga, a feat that made the tsar seek his service.
britannica-1911-ortelius-abraham:
Abraham Ortelius, born at Antwerp in fifteen twenty seven, was next to Mercator the greatest geographer of his age, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. His family came from Augsburg in Germany. He travelled widely in western Europe, in the Netherlands, Germany, France, England, and Italy.

He began as a map engraver, joining the Antwerp painters' gild in fifteen forty seven. His early career was that of a business man, with yearly trips to the Frankfurt fair. In fifteen sixty a trip with Mercator turned him to science. At his friend's urging he set out to compile an atlas, the Theatre of the World. A world map came first in fifteen sixty four. The full atlas was issued in fifteen seventy.
britannica-1911-oughtred-william:
William Oughtred is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English mathematician. He lived from 1575 to 1660, the text notes. He was born at Eton and schooled there. He went on to King's College, Cambridge, and became a fellow. He took holy orders and left the university about 1603. He then held a church post near Guildford in Surrey.

About 1628 the earl of Arundel set him to teach his son. His house drew pupils from far and wide. He wrote to the top scholars of his day on maths. His Clavis book of 1631 brought in new signs for maths work. A book on navigation followed in 1632. He also wrote on the use of dials and on trig sums. He died, it is said, in joy at the king's return.
britannica-1911-page-william:
William Page, an American artist who lived from 1811 to 1885, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Albany in New York, he first studied for the ministry at Andover. In later life he became a Swedenborgian in faith. His art training came from Morse and from the schools of the National Academy of Design.

Page became a National Academician in 1836 and lived in Rome from 1849 to 1860. In Rome he painted portraits of his friends Robert and Elizabeth Browning. He led the National Academy of Design as president from 1871 to 1873. Portraits fill most of his work, with a few famed subject pieces. One shows Admiral Farragut at the battle of Mobile and belonged to the tsar of Russia. He also modelled and painted heads of Shakespeare from a death mask, and wrote on how to measure the human figure.
britannica-1911-palfrey-john-gorham:
John Gorham Palfrey (1796–1881) was an American historian, and a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his many posts. He was born in Boston, Massachusetts, on the second of May 1796. He graduated at Harvard in 1815 and became a Unitarian minister. He served as pastor of the Brattle Square church in Boston from 1818 to 1831.

Palfrey taught sacred literature at the Harvard divinity school through the 1830s. He edited the North American Review from 1835 to 1843. Public office followed, as secretary of state of Massachusetts and then as a member of Congress. He was postmaster of Boston from 1861 to 1867. As a writer he is best known for his History of New England. That work ran to five volumes, the last issued after his death in 1890.
britannica-1911-pasley-sir-charles-willi:
Sir Charles William Pasley, who lived from 1780 to 1861, was a British army engineer. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth in Dumfriesshire. He entered the Woolwich academy in 1796 and won his commission a year later. He fought at Gaeta, Maida, and Copenhagen. In Spain he served on staff thanks to his grasp of Spanish. A grave wound at Flushing ended his field service.

The rest of his life went to one great task. He built a full science of army engineering and a trained corps to match. The war office took up his views after the Spanish war showed the need. In 1812 he was put at the head of the new school at Woolwich. He was still only a captain at the time. His course of army instruction came out in three volumes by 1817.
britannica-1911-paterson-william:
William Paterson (1658–1719) was a British writer on finance, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica names his two great projects. He was the founder of the Bank of England. He was also the projector of the Darien scheme. Paterson was born in April 1658 at a farmhouse in Dumfriesshire.

His parents farmed at Skipmyre in the parish of Tinwald. He lived with them until he was about seventeen years old. A wish to escape the religious persecution then raging in Scotland drove him south. He crossed England with a pedlar’s pack on his back. He settled for a time in Bristol, then went on to America. There he lived mainly in the Bahamas. Some said he had been a preacher there, and others a buccaneer.
britannica-1911-paynter-william:
William Paynter (c. 1540–1594), also spelled Painter, was an English author from Kent. He entered St John's College, Cambridge, in 1554. In 1561 he became clerk of the ordnance in the Tower of London. In that post he seems to have grown rich on public funds. In 1586 he owned that he owed the state a thousand pounds, and more charges of theft from office came the next year.

Paynter's son Anthony owned in 1591 that both of them had abused their trust. Yet Paynter kept his post until his death, which came soon after his will of February 1594. His Palace of Pleasure came out in 1566, with sixty tales, and a second volume with thirty-four more tales came in 1567. A new edition in 1575 added seven tales. He drew tales from Herodotus, Plutarch, Livy, and Tacitus, and from Italian writers such as Bandello.
britannica-1911-peach-charles-william:
Charles William Peach (1800-1886) was a British naturalist and geologist who learned his science on coastguard duty, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells his story. He was born at Wansford in Northamptonshire, the son of a saddler who later kept an inn and farmed. After a plain schooling he helped in the inn and on the farm. In 1824 he became a riding officer in the Revenue Coast-guard at Weybourn in Norfolk.

Seaweeds and other shore life caught his eye there, and he collected them with zeal. His duties moved him along the Norfolk coast from town to town. On his rounds he met a curate who lent him books and set his growing knowledge on firm ground. About 1830 he was moved to Dorset, then to Devon and to Cornwall, collecting all the way and sending specimens to working naturalists.
britannica-1911-pelham:
Pelham is the name of an English family drawn from a place of that name in Hertfordshire. The 1911 Britannica entry says a man of the name held that place under an early king, and tale claims the house held it before the Norman conquest of England.

The entry lists the high ranks the house won over the ages: a barony, earldoms, and a dukedom, some now dead lines and some still held. It then turns to the early men of the house. One helped take a French king in battle and gained land by a good match. His son served a great duke and his son the king, held a key castle post for life, was made a knight at a crowning, and sat in the Commons many times.
britannica-1911-pengelly-william:
William Pengelly, an English geologist and student of early man, was born at East Looe in Cornwall in eighteen twelve. His father captained a small coasting ship. Pengelly began life as a sailor after a plain schooling in his village. In eighteen twenty eight he left the sea for good. A love of learning had grown in him, and he moved to Torquay to teach.

At Torquay he started a school, then tutored pupils in maths and natural science. Geology had drawn him since his youth, and he took it up in earnest at about thirty. He helped refound a mechanics institute and start a natural history society. He also helped found a Devon group for learning, science, and art. His fossil finds from Devon and Cornwall went to the Oxford Museum in eighteen sixty.
britannica-1911-pepperrell-sir-william:
Sir William Pepperrell was an American soldier of the colonial era in Maine. He lived from sixteen ninety six to seventeen fifty nine. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Kittery, Maine, he studied surveying and sea craft in youth.

Pepperrell joined his father in ship building, fishing, and general trade work. He soon ranked among the richest and strongest men in the province. He rose through militia ranks to colonel by seventeen twenty six. In seventeen forty five he led New England troops against Louisburg fort. With a British fleet he forced the French fort to yield that June. Britain made him a baronet, the sole New Englander so honoured.
britannica-1911-petre-sir-william:
Sir William Petre, an English statesman of Tudor times, gets a life in the 1911 Britannica. Born near fifteen oh five, he was a Devon man taught at Oxford. He held a post at All Souls College there. At Oxford he had taught the brother of Anne Boleyn. That link may have brought him into state work while still young. In fifteen thirty six he served as aide to Thomas Cromwell.

He was knighted and made a chief clerk of state in fifteen forty three. He kept his post through the reigns of Edward and Mary by deft shifts of side. He backed the match of Mary with Philip of Spain. He quit his post in fifteen fifty seven and died in Essex in fifteen seventy two. Kin notes trace his line on.
britannica-1911-phillips-william:
William Phillips, who lived from 1775 to 1828, was a British student of minerals and rocks. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born in London on the tenth of May 1775. His father was a printer and bookseller there. Phillips took an early love for the two fields and helped found the Geological Society of London in 1807. His first books on minerals came out in 1815 and 1816 and became set texts.

His larger work on the rocks of England and Wales was done with Conybeare. Only the first part came out, in 1822, but the article rates it very high. It calls the book a model of close field work and clear order. Phillips was a member of the Society of Friends. He joined the Royal Society in 1827, one year before his death.
britannica-1911-pinkney-william:
William Pinkney, an American lawyer and statesman who lived from 1764 to 1822, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Annapolis in Maryland and joined the bar in 1786. He sat in the state meeting that ratified the federal compact for Maryland. He served in the state house and on its council in his early years.

From 1796 to 1804 he sat on a board set up by the Jay treaty to weigh claims by American merchants for ships seized in war. In 1806 he and James Monroe were sent to treat with Britain on the seizure of neutral ships. He then served as minister in London until 1811. He was attorney-general of the United States from 1811 to 1814 and was wounded at Bladensburg. Later posts took him to Russia and Naples.
britannica-1911-pole-william:
William Pole was an English builder of works who lived from eighteen fourteen to nineteen hundred. He was born at Birmingham and held build posts in England in his youth. In eighteen forty-four he went to India to teach build craft. Ill health forced him home in four years.

In London he won a high name and took the chair of build craft at a chief school. State work came in bulk, on ship plate, guns, rails, and the water of London. He also gave word on a new rifle and on rails in Japan. Song was a twin love, and he wrote a book on its thought.
britannica-1911-pram:
Pram is defined in a brief entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from the Dutch praam. It names a flat bottomed boat or barge used as a lighter. Such craft load and unload cargo in the ports of the Baltic and North Sea.

The entry spends most of its space on the word itself. Forms of it are common in all the tongues round those seas. At root it is Slavonic in form. Its deep source links to a wide set of words for going through or travel. The text sets it by fare, ferry, and far, and by Greek and Latin kin words for a way and for carry. Though tiny, the note gives both the thing and its name a clear place. It will serve any reader who meets the term in sea trade texts.
britannica-1911-rashbam:
Rashbam is a short life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a medieval Jewish scholar of France. The name is formed from the initials of Rabbi Samuel ben Meir (1085 to 1174). He stood among the leaders of the French school of Bible study. A grandson of Rashi, he parted from his grandfather in method and wrote notes on the Pentateuch and other Scripture.

Rashbam followed a plain, natural way of reading the text rather than the homiletic one. On Genesis he held that the day begins at dawn, not at sunset. On a hard phrase in Genesis he read the words as Until he cometh to Shiloh and tied them to the split of the kingdom of Judah after Solomon. His Bible notes are brief; his Talmud notes, on several tracts, are noted for length.
britannica-1911-ream: Ream is a set quantity of paper, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains in brief. A ream is 20 quires of 24 sheets each, or 480 sheets in all. A printer ream is larger, at 516 sheets to the bundle. The word came into Europe through the Moors, who began the paper making of Spain. Its source is an Arabic word for a bale or bundle, and its first meaning was simply bundle, for paper or for clothes alike.
britannica-1911-rimmer-william:
William Rimmer, an American artist who lived from 1816 to 1879, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Liverpool, England, the son of a French refugee. The family moved to Nova Scotia in 1818 and then to Boston in 1826. His father made shoes there, and the boy learned the trade too.

Rimmer worked at turns as a draughtsman, a sign painter, a portrait painter, and even a doctor. In 1860 he made a head of St Stephen, and in 1861 his Falling Gladiator won high praise. One critic called it the most striking work of sculpture yet made in the country. Most of his work was soon lost. He built his forms up in clay and cut them back, working fast and with few tools.
britannica-1911-robertson-thomas-william:
Robertson, Thomas William is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English actor and dramatist. He was the son of a provincial actor-manager, and knew the stage from childhood. His success came late. After years in the provinces he reached London in 1860.

David Garrick, played at the Haymarket, was his first marked success. Society, at the Prince of Wales's Theatre, then revealed a new kind of play. Critics sneered at cup-and-saucer comedy, but London flocked to the little house, and imitations flooded the stage. The article lists the plays that followed year by year: Ours, Caste, Play, School and M P. Robertson died in 1871, at the height of a brief and brilliant fame.
britannica-1911-robertson-william:
William Robertson is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a Scottish historian. He lived from 1721 to 1793. He was born at Borthwick in Mid Lothian. He was the eldest son of a minister of the same name. He was schooled at Dalkeith and at Edinburgh university. From the first he was meant for the ministry. In 1743 he was given the living of Gladsmuir. Two years later both his parents died within hours.

The care of a brother and six sisters fell to him. His income then was less than a hundred pounds a year. His love of study never cut into his parish duties. His power as a preacher made him a local name. The rebellion of 1745 brought out his energy and decision. Edinburgh seemed in danger of falling to the rebels then. The entry goes on to his rise as a historian.
britannica-1911-rogers-william:
William Rogers, an English church man and school reformer born in eighteen nineteen, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London, the son of a law man, he was schooled at Eton and at Oxford. He then read church study at Durham and was ordained in eighteen forty three.

In eighteen forty five he took a poor parish in London and stayed eighteen years. He threw himself into school work for his poor and rough flock. He began with a class for ragged boys in a shed left by a smith. With help from friends he grew the work till the whole parish was a web of schools. In eighteen fifty eight he sat on a royal probe of mass schooling. When a new school law passed, London chose him for its school board. The entry shows faith and schooling fused in one tireless life.
britannica-1911-roscoe-william:
William Roscoe, an English historian and writer, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Liverpool in seventeen fifty three, he was the son of a market gardener who kept a public house. Roscoe was eager for knowledge from a young age. At twelve he left school, having learned all his master could teach.

He then helped his father in the garden and gave his free hours to reading and study. In his own words that life gave health to his body and food to his mind. He recalled the deep sleep that followed his labour with fondness. The entry follows his rise from that plain start to literary fame.
britannica-1911-rotherham:
Rotherham is a market town and borough in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England, five miles north-east of Sheffield. The 1911 Britannica article gives its count as 54,349 in 1901, up from 42,061 in 1891. The town lies in the valley of the Don, where the Rother stream joins it. A bridge with an old chapel on it spans the river. Three rail lines serve the town, and boats reach the Humber by water.

The parish church of All Saints stands on a Saxon site and was built in the reign of Edward the Fourth. Critics count it among the best Perpendicular churches in the north. Iron, steel, and brass works lead the town trades. Wagon works, potteries, glass works, and breweries add to the list. The borough was formed in 1871, on an area of 6,012 acres. A Roman fort once stood at Templeborough near by.
britannica-1911-rotterdam:
Rotterdam is a city of Holland in the province of South Holland, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces its rise as a port. It stands on both banks of the New Maas where the canalised Rotte joins it. Its people grew from about twenty thousand in 1632 to 379,017 in 1905. Its shipping works have raised it to the first place among the trading cities of Holland.

The New Waterway, built from 1869 to 1890 out to the Hook of Holland, lets the largest ships reach it. Its chief quay, the Boompjes, lines the north bank of the river. The city first stood only on that north bank. In 1869 it spread to the south shore by taking in Feienoord, and later it absorbed Delftshaven, Charlois, and Kralingen.
britannica-1911-russell-lord-william:
Lord William Russell, an English politician who lived from 1639 to 1683, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the third son of the first duke of Bedford and was born in September 1639. About 1654 he was sent to Cambridge with his elder brother. On the death of that brother in 1678, he gained the courtesy title of Lord Russell.

After university the brothers travelled abroad, visiting Lyons and Geneva and living for a while at Augsburg. William's account of what he saw is lively and of interest, the entry says. At the Restoration he was elected for the family borough of Tavistock. For a long time he took no part in public affairs, the article notes. He gave those years to the follies of court life and was twice drawn into duels.
britannica-1911-sacheverell-william:
William Sacheverell, an English statesman, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in sixteen thirty eight, he was the son of a country gentleman. His family had held a good place in Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire for centuries. He inherited large estates from his father.

He was admitted at Gray's Inn and in sixteen seventy was elected to Parliament for Derbyshire. He at once gained a leading place in the party opposed to the court. Within six months he proposed that all Catholic recusants be removed from military posts. The entry follows his role as a sharp voice against royal policy in the Commons.
britannica-1911-senior-nassau-william:
Nassau William Senior, an English economist who lived from 1790 to 1864, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Compton in Berkshire in September 1790, he was the eldest son of a Wiltshire vicar. He was taught at Eton and at Magdalen College, Oxford. At Oxford he was a private pupil of Richard Whately, a lifelong friend. He took his degree in 1811 and was called to the bar in 1819.

In 1825 Senior was elected to the new Oxford chair of political economy, which he held twice. Lord Melbourne asked him in 1830 to inquire into combinations and strikes. He sat on the Poor Law Inquiry Commission of 1832. He also served on the Handloom Weavers Commission, whose report he drew up. In 1861 he joined the inquiry into popular education.
britannica-1911-sherlock-william:
William Sherlock was an English church man who lived from about sixteen forty-one to seventeen seven. He was born at Southwark and schooled at Eton and at Cambridge. He took a London church post in sixteen sixty-nine. A bent for sharp dispute showed in his first books.

One book set out when men may fight a kings rule and when they must yield in peace. That split was held by most high church men of his day. He lost his post for a time past the great change, for he would not swear to the new pair. A book on death from those years sold wide.
britannica-1911-shoreham:
Shoreham, a seaport in Sussex, England, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands near the mouth of the river Adur, six miles west of Brighton by rail. Its urban district held 3,837 people in 1901. The town is often called New Shoreham, to set it apart from Old Shoreham village. That village, a mile up the river, was the former port.

The church of St Mary the Virgin has lost almost its whole nave. What remains shows fine work from Norman to Early English. The church of St Nicholas at Old Shoreham is a cross-shaped Norman building with notable early woodwork. Public gardens hold a museum and a theatre. The small port trades chiefly in coal, corn, and timber, and shipbuilding goes on. The article notes a boys' school near the town and traces the port's early rise to its natural harbour.
britannica-1911-simon-abraham:
Abraham Simon, who lived from 1622 to 1692, was an English medallist and modeller born in Yorkshire. The 1911 Britannica article says he was meant for the church at first. He turned to art, learned in Holland, and went on to Sweden. Queen Christina took him into her service there, and he travelled with her train to Paris. He came back to England before the Civil War broke out.

Simon won fame for medals and for portraits modelled in wax. In the Commonwealth years he made medals of its chief men. At the Restoration, Charles the Second gave him a hundred guineas for a royal portrait. That medal was meant for a planned order of the Royal Oak. A clash with the duke of York cost him the court's favour. He died in neglect in 1692. His brother Thomas chased many of his medals.
britannica-1911-skeat-walter-william:
Walter William Skeat (1835-), an English scholar of language, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London, he was schooled at King's College and at Highgate Grammar School, then at Christ's College in Cambridge. He became a fellow there in July 1860. In 1878 he was chosen as professor of Anglo-Saxon at Cambridge.

The article says he finished another man's edition of the Anglo-Saxon Gospels and did much work in Anglo-Saxon and in Gothic. He is best known, though, for his work in Middle English. His standard editions covered Chaucer and Piers Plowman. A joint Oxford plan for Chaucer fell through when his partner's drive failed. Skeat later took the task up alone and brought out the work in six books in 1894, with a seventh book of Chaucerian pieces in 1897.
britannica-1911-smith-george-adam:
George Adam Smith was a Scottish divine born in Calcutta in eighteen fifty six. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father George Smith was head of Doveton College in Calcutta then. The son was schooled at Edinburgh in high school, university, and New College.

Smith studied at Tubingen and Leipzig and travelled in Egypt and Syria. He joined the Free Church of Scotland ministry after those travels abroad. In eighteen ninety two he became a teacher of Old Testament studies at Glasgow. In nineteen o nine he was made head of the University of Aberdeen. His works include books on Isaiah, on Jerusalem, and on Holy Land lands.
britannica-1911-smith-sir-william:
Sir William Smith (1813–1893) was an English lexicographer, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his turn from law to classics. He was born at Enfield in 1813, of Nonconformist parents. He was first meant for a career in theology. Instead he was articled to a solicitor as a young man.

In his spare time Smith taught himself the classics on his own. At University College he carried off both the Greek and the Latin prizes. He gave up his legal studies for a post at University College school. There he began to write on classical subjects. He next turned his hand to lexicography, the making of dictionaries. His first try was the Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities, issued in 1842. He wrote the greater part of that work himself.
britannica-1911-smyth-william:
